<p><i><b>Scooby-Doo</b></i> (often written as <i><b>Scooby-Doo!</b></i>) is an American <a href="/wiki/Media_franchise" title="Media franchise">media franchise</a> owned by <a href="/wiki/Warner_Bros." title="Warner Bros.">Warner Bros. Entertainment</a> and created in 1969 by writers <a href="/wiki/Joe_Ruby" title="Joe Ruby">Joe Ruby</a> and <a href="/wiki/Ken_Spears" title="Ken Spears">Ken Spears</a> through their <a href="/wiki/Animated_series" title="Animated series">animated series</a>, <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo,_Where_Are_You!" title="Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!">Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!</a></i>, for <a href="/wiki/Hanna-Barbera" title="Hanna-Barbera">Hanna-Barbera</a>, which was later absorbed into <a href="/wiki/Warner_Bros._Animation" title="Warner Bros. Animation">Warner Bros. Animation</a> in 2001. The series features four teenagers: <a href="/wiki/Fred_Jones_(Scooby-Doo)" title="Fred Jones (Scooby-Doo)">Fred Jones</a>, <a href="/wiki/Daphne_Blake" title="Daphne Blake">Daphne Blake</a>, <a href="/wiki/Velma_Dinkley" title="Velma Dinkley">Velma Dinkley</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Shaggy_Rogers" title="Shaggy Rogers">Shaggy Rogers</a>, and their talking <a href="/wiki/Great_Dane" title="Great Dane">Great Dane</a>, <a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo_(character)" title="Scooby-Doo (character)">Scooby-Doo</a>, who solve mysteries involving supposedly supernatural creatures through a series of antics and missteps, while traveling in a brightly colored van called the <i>Mystery Machine</i>. The franchise has numerous shows, films, and specials.<sup id="cite_ref-ReferenceA_1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ReferenceA-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p><i>Scooby-Doo</i> was originally broadcast on <a href="/wiki/CBS" title="CBS">CBS</a> from 1969 to 1976, when it moved to <a href="/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company" title="American Broadcasting Company">ABC</a>. ABC aired various versions of <i>Scooby-Doo</i> until canceling it in 1986, and presented a <a href="/wiki/Spin-off_(media)" class="mw-redirect" title="Spin-off (media)">spin-off</a> featuring the characters as children called <i><a href="/wiki/A_Pup_Named_Scooby-Doo" title="A Pup Named Scooby-Doo">A Pup Named Scooby-Doo</a></i> from 1988 to 1991. Two <i>Scooby-Doo</i> reboots aired as part of <a href="/wiki/Kids%27_WB" title="Kids' WB">Kids' WB</a> on <a href="/wiki/The_WB" title="The WB">The WB</a> and its successor <a href="/wiki/The_CW" title="The CW">The CW</a> from 2002 to 2008. Further reboots aired on <a href="/wiki/Cartoon_Network" title="Cartoon Network">Cartoon Network</a> from 2010 to 2018. Repeats of the various <i>Scooby-Doo</i> series are frequently broadcast on Cartoon Network's sister channel <a href="/wiki/Boomerang_(TV_network)" title="Boomerang (TV network)">Boomerang</a> in the United States and other countries. The most recent <i>Scooby-Doo</i> series, <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo_and_Guess_Who%3F" title="Scooby-Doo and Guess Who?">Scooby-Doo and Guess Who?</a></i>, premiered on June 27, 2019, as an original series on <a href="/wiki/Boomerang_(TV_network)#Availability_on_subscription_television" title="Boomerang (TV network)">Boomerang's streaming service</a> and later <a href="/wiki/HBO_Max" title="HBO Max">HBO Max</a>.
</p><p>In 2013, <i><a href="/wiki/TV_Guide" title="TV Guide">TV Guide</a></i> ranked <i>Scooby-Doo</i> the fifth-greatest TV cartoon of all time.<sup id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>

<p>In 1968, <a href="/wiki/Consumer_organization" title="Consumer organization">parent-run organizations</a>, particularly <a href="/wiki/Action_for_Children%27s_Television" title="Action for Children's Television">Action for Children's Television</a> (ACT), began protesting what they perceived as excessive violence in Saturday-morning cartoons.<sup id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Most of these shows were <a href="/wiki/Hanna-Barbera" title="Hanna-Barbera">Hanna-Barbera</a> action cartoons such as <i><a href="/wiki/Space_Ghost_(TV_series)" title="Space Ghost (TV series)">Space Ghost</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/The_Herculoids" title="The Herculoids">The Herculoids</a></i>, and <i><a href="/wiki/Birdman_and_the_Galaxy_Trio" title="Birdman and the Galaxy Trio">Birdman and the Galaxy Trio</a></i>, and virtually all of them were canceled by 1969 because of pressure from the parent groups.<sup id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Members of these watch groups served as advisers to Hanna-Barbera and other animation studios to ensure that new programs would be safe for children.
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Fred_Silverman" title="Fred Silverman">Fred Silverman</a>, an executive for <a href="/wiki/Daytime_television_in_the_United_States" title="Daytime television in the United States">daytime programming</a> at <a href="/wiki/CBS" title="CBS">CBS</a>, was then looking for a show that would both revitalize his Saturday-morning line and please the watch groups. The result was <i><a href="/wiki/The_Archie_Show" title="The Archie Show">The Archie Show</a></i> from <a href="/wiki/Filmation" title="Filmation">Filmation</a>, based on <a href="/wiki/Bob_Montana" title="Bob Montana">Bob Montana</a>'s teenage humor comic book <i><a href="/wiki/Archie_(comic_book)" title="Archie (comic book)">Archie</a></i>. Also successful were the musical numbers <a href="/wiki/The_Archies" title="The Archies">The Archies</a> performed during each program (one of which, "<a href="/wiki/Sugar,_Sugar" title="Sugar, Sugar">Sugar, Sugar</a>", was the most successful <i><a href="/wiki/Billboard_magazine" class="mw-redirect" title="Billboard magazine">Billboard</a></i> <a href="/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100" title="Billboard Hot 100">number-one hit</a> of 1969). Eager to build upon this success, Silverman contacted producers <a href="/wiki/William_Hanna" title="William Hanna">William Hanna</a> and <a href="/wiki/Joseph_Barbera" title="Joseph Barbera">Joseph Barbera</a> about creating another show based on a teenage rock group, this time featuring teens who solved mysteries between gigs. Silverman envisioned the show as a cross between the popular <i><a href="/wiki/I_Love_a_Mystery" title="I Love a Mystery">I Love a Mystery</a></i> <a href="/wiki/Old-time_radio" class="mw-redirect" title="Old-time radio">radio</a> <a href="/wiki/Radio_drama" title="Radio drama">serials</a> of the 1940s and the Archie characters or the popular early 1960s television series <i><a href="/wiki/The_Many_Loves_of_Dobie_Gillis" title="The Many Loves of Dobie Gillis">The Many Loves of Dobie Gillis</a></i>.<sup id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-5"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>After attempting to develop his version of the show, called <i>House of Mystery</i>,<sup id="cite_ref-STUEP1_6-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-STUEP1-6"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Barbera, who developed and sold Hanna-Barbera shows while Hanna produced them,<sup id="cite_ref-STUEP1_6-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-STUEP1-6"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> passed the task along to story writers <a href="/wiki/Joe_Ruby" title="Joe Ruby">Joe Ruby</a> and <a href="/wiki/Ken_Spears" title="Ken Spears">Ken Spears</a>, as well as artist/character designer <a href="/wiki/Iwao_Takamoto" title="Iwao Takamoto">Iwao Takamoto</a>. Their treatment, based in part on <i>The Archie Show</i>, was titled <i>Mysteries Five</i> and featured five teenagers: Geoff, Mike, Kelly, Linda, and Linda's brother W.W., along with their <a href="/wiki/Bongo_drum" title="Bongo drum">bongo</a>-playing dog, Too Much, who collectively formed the band Mysteries Five. When The Mysteries Five were not performing at gigs, they were out solving spooky mysteries involving ghosts, <a href="/wiki/Zombie" title="Zombie">zombies</a>, and other supernatural creatures. Ruby and Spears were unable to decide whether Too Much would be a large cowardly dog or a small feisty one.<sup id="cite_ref-STUEP1_6-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-STUEP1-6"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> When the former was chosen, Ruby and Spears wrote Too Much as a <a href="/wiki/Great_Dane" title="Great Dane">Great Dane</a> but revised the dog character to a large <a href="/wiki/Old_English_Sheepdog" title="Old English Sheepdog">sheepdog</a> (similar to the Archies' sheepdog, <a href="/wiki/Hot_Dog_(comics)" class="mw-redirect" title="Hot Dog (comics)">Hot Dog</a>) just before their presentation to Silverman, as Ruby feared the character would be too similar to the comic strip character <a href="/wiki/Marmaduke" title="Marmaduke">Marmaduke</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-STUEP1_6-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-STUEP1-6"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Silverman rejected their initial pitch, and after consulting with Barbera on next steps, got Barbera's permission to go ahead with Too Much being a Great Dane instead of a sheepdog.<sup id="cite_ref-STUEP1_6-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-STUEP1-6"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-RubyAndSpears_7-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-RubyAndSpears-7"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>7<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>During the design phase, lead character designer Takamoto consulted a studio colleague who was a <a href="/wiki/Dog_breeding" title="Dog breeding">breeder</a> of Great Danes. After learning the characteristics of a prize-winning Great Dane from her, Takamoto proceeded to break most of the rules and designed Too Much with overly bowed legs, a <a href="/wiki/Double_chin" class="mw-redirect" title="Double chin">double chin</a>, and a sloped back, among other abnormalities.<sup id="cite_ref-8" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-8"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-9" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-9"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Ruby and Spears' second pass at the show used <i>Dobie Gillis</i> as the template for the teenagers rather than <i>Archie</i>. The treatment retained the dog Too Much, while reducing the number of teenagers to four, removing the Mike character and retaining Geoff, Kelly, Linda, and W.W.<sup id="cite_ref-RubyAndSpears_7-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-RubyAndSpears-7"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>7<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Their personalities were modified, so were the characters' names: Geoff became "Ronnie"<sup id="cite_ref-10" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-10"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>10<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>—later renamed "<a href="/wiki/Fred_Jones_(Scooby-Doo)" title="Fred Jones (Scooby-Doo)">Fred</a>" (at Silverman's behest),<sup id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-11"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>11<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Kelly became "<a href="/wiki/Daphne_Blake" title="Daphne Blake">Daphne</a>", Linda "<a href="/wiki/Velma_Dinkley" title="Velma Dinkley">Velma</a>", and W.W. "<a href="/wiki/Shaggy_Rogers" title="Shaggy Rogers">Shaggy</a>". The teens were now based on four teenage characters from <i>The Many Loves of Dobie Gillis</i>: <a href="/wiki/Dobie_Gillis" class="mw-redirect" title="Dobie Gillis">Dobie Gillis</a>, Thalia Menninger, <a href="/wiki/Zelda_Gilroy" title="Zelda Gilroy">Zelda Gilroy</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Maynard_G._Krebs" title="Maynard G. Krebs">Maynard G. Krebs</a>, respectively.<sup id="cite_ref-STUEP1_6-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-STUEP1-6"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-12" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-12"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>12<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-jbarberainterviewvideo_13-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-jbarberainterviewvideo-13"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>13<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The revised show was re-pitched to Silverman, who liked the material but, disliking the title <i>Mysteries Five</i>, decided to call the show "<i>Who's S-S-Scared?</i>".<sup id="cite_ref-fsilvermanvideo_14-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-fsilvermanvideo-14"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>14<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Silverman presented <i>Who's S-S-Scared?</i> to the CBS executives as the centerpiece for the upcoming 1969–70 season's Saturday-morning cartoon block. CBS president <a href="/wiki/Frank_Stanton_(executive)" title="Frank Stanton (executive)">Frank Stanton</a> felt that the presentation artwork was too scary for young viewers and, thinking the show would be the same, decided to pass on it.<sup id="cite_ref-RubyAndSpears_7-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-RubyAndSpears-7"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>7<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-fsilvermanvideo_14-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-fsilvermanvideo-14"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>14<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Now without a centerpiece for the upcoming season's programming, Silverman had Ruby, Spears, and the Hanna-Barbera staff revise the treatments and presentation materials to tone down the show and better reflect its comedy elements. The rock band element was dropped, and more attention was focused on Shaggy and Too Much. According to Ruby and Spears, Silverman was inspired by <a href="/wiki/Frank_Sinatra" title="Frank Sinatra">Frank Sinatra</a>'s <a href="/wiki/Scat_singing" title="Scat singing">scat</a> "doo-be-doo-be-doo" at the end of his recording of "<a href="/wiki/Strangers_in_the_Night" title="Strangers in the Night">Strangers in the Night</a>" on a <a href="/wiki/Red-eye_flight" title="Red-eye flight">red-eye flight</a> to one of the development meetings, and decided to rename the dog "<a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo_(character)" title="Scooby-Doo (character)">Scooby-Doo</a>" and retitled the show "<i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo,_Where_Are_You!" title="Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!">Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!</a></i>".<sup id="cite_ref-RubyAndSpears_7-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-RubyAndSpears-7"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>7<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-15"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>15<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The revised show was re-presented to CBS executives, who approved it for production.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="CBS_years_(1969–76)"><span id="CBS_years_.281969.E2.80.9376.29"></span>CBS years (1969–76)</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: CBS years (1969–76)"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Scooby-doo-meddling-kids-1970.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/3/3c/Scooby-doo-meddling-kids-1970.jpg/250px-Scooby-doo-meddling-kids-1970.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="187" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/3/3c/Scooby-doo-meddling-kids-1970.jpg 2x" data-file-width="300" data-file-height="225"></a><figcaption>Every episode of the original <i>Scooby-Doo</i> format contains a penultimate scene in which the heroes unmask the seemingly supernatural antagonist to reveal a real person in a costume, as in this scene from "Nowhere to Hyde", an episode of <i>Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!</i>, originally aired on CBS on September 12, 1970.</figcaption></figure>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Scooby-Doo,_Where_Are_You!"><span id="Scooby-Doo.2C_Where_Are_You.21"></span><i>Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!</i></h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>The first episode of <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo,_Where_Are_You!" title="Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!">Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!</a></i>, "What a Night for a Knight", debuted on the CBS network Saturday, September 13, 1969, at 10:30 AM Eastern Time. The original <a href="/wiki/Voice_acting" title="Voice acting">voice cast</a> featured <a href="/wiki/Don_Messick" title="Don Messick">Don Messick</a> as Scooby-Doo, <a href="/wiki/Casey_Kasem" title="Casey Kasem">Casey Kasem</a> as Shaggy, <a href="/wiki/Frank_Welker" title="Frank Welker">Frank Welker</a> as Fred, actress <a href="/wiki/Nicole_Jaffe" title="Nicole Jaffe">Nicole Jaffe</a> as Velma, and <a href="/wiki/Indira_Stefanianna" title="Indira Stefanianna">Indira Stefanianna</a> as Daphne.<sup id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-16"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>16<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Scooby's speech patterns closely resembled an earlier cartoon dog, <a href="/wiki/Astro_(The_Jetsons)" class="mw-redirect" title="Astro (The Jetsons)">Astro</a> from <i><a href="/wiki/The_Jetsons" title="The Jetsons">The Jetsons</a></i> (1962–63), also voiced by Messick.<sup id="cite_ref-ReferenceA_1-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ReferenceA-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Seventeen episodes of <i>Scooby-Doo Where Are You!</i> were produced in 1969–70. The series theme song was written by David Mook and Ben Raleigh, and performed by Larry Marks.
</p><p>Each of these episodes features Scooby and the four teenage members of Mystery, Inc.: <a href="/wiki/Fred_Jones_(Scooby-Doo)" title="Fred Jones (Scooby-Doo)">Fred</a>, <a href="/wiki/Shaggy_Rogers" title="Shaggy Rogers">Shaggy</a>, <a href="/wiki/Daphne_Blake" title="Daphne Blake">Daphne</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Velma_Dinkley" title="Velma Dinkley">Velma</a>, arriving at a location in the Mystery Machine, a van painted with <a href="/wiki/Psychedelic_color" class="mw-redirect" title="Psychedelic color">psychedelic colors</a> and <a href="/wiki/Flower_power" title="Flower power">flower power</a> imagery. Encountering a purportedly supernatural monster terrorizing the local populace, such as a ghost, they decide to investigate. The kids split up to look for clues and suspects, while being chased at turns by the monster. Eventually, the kids come to realize the paranormal activity is actually an elaborate hoax, and—often with the help of a <a href="/wiki/Rube_Goldberg" title="Rube Goldberg">Rube Goldberg</a>-like trap designed by Fred—they capture the <a href="/wiki/Creature_suit" title="Creature suit">creature suit</a>-wearing villain and unmask him or her. Revealed usually as a flesh and blood crook who used the costume to cover up their crimes, the villain is arrested and taken to jail, often with the catchphrase "if it weren't for those pesky/meddling kids!". A few times though, the "villain" turns out to be innocent, such as a haywire robot or the owner disguised to scare away thieves.<sup id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-17"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>17<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>  However, in all cases, the 'supernatural' element of the mystery was revealed to be phony -- in the end, there were no <i>actual</i> ghosts or monsters featured on the show.
</p><p>Scheduled opposite another teenage mystery-solving show, ABC's <i><a href="/wiki/The_Hardy_Boys_(1969_TV_series)" title="The Hardy Boys (1969 TV series)">The Hardy Boys</a></i>, <i>Scooby-Doo</i> became a ratings success, with <a href="/wiki/Nielsen_ratings" class="mw-redirect" title="Nielsen ratings">Nielsen ratings</a> reporting that as many as 65% of Saturday-morning audiences were tuned in to CBS when <i>Scooby-Doo</i> was being broadcast.<sup id="cite_ref-STUEP1_6-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-STUEP1-6"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-RubyAndSpears_7-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-RubyAndSpears-7"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>7<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The show was renewed for a second season in 1970, for which eight episodes were produced. Seven of the second-season episodes featured chase sequences set to <a href="/wiki/Bubblegum_pop" class="mw-redirect" title="Bubblegum pop">bubblegum pop</a> songs recorded by <a href="/wiki/Austin_Roberts_(singer)" title="Austin Roberts (singer)">Austin Roberts</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>18<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> who also re-recorded the theme song for this season. With Stefanianna Christopherson having married and retired from voice acting, <a href="/wiki/Heather_North" title="Heather North">Heather North</a> assumed the role of Daphne, and she continued to voice the character until 1997.<sup id="cite_ref-19" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-19"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>19<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The TV influences of <i><a href="/wiki/I_Love_a_Mystery" title="I Love a Mystery">I Love a Mystery</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/The_Many_Loves_of_Dobie_Gillis" title="The Many Loves of Dobie Gillis">Dobie Gillis</a></i> were apparent in the first episode. Of the similarities between the <i>Scooby-Doo</i> teens and the <i>Dobie Gillis</i> teens, the similarities between Shaggy and Maynard are the most noticeable; both characters share the same <a href="/wiki/Beatnik" title="Beatnik">beatnik</a>-style <a href="/wiki/Goatee" title="Goatee">goatee</a>, similar hairstyles, and demeanors.<sup id="cite_ref-STUEP1_6-7" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-STUEP1-6"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The core premise of <i>Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!</i> was also similar to <a href="/wiki/Enid_Blyton" title="Enid Blyton">Enid Blyton</a>'s <i><a href="/wiki/The_Famous_Five" title="The Famous Five">Famous Five</a></i> books. Both series featured four youths with a dog, and the Famous Five stories often revolved around a mystery which invariably turned out not to be supernaturally based, but simply a ruse to <a href="/wiki/Disguise" title="Disguise">disguise</a> the villain's true intent.
</p><p>The role of each character was strongly defined in the series: Fred is the leader and the determined detective, Velma is the intelligent analyst, Daphne is danger-prone, Shaggy is a coward more motivated by hunger than any desire to solve mysteries, and Scooby is similar to Shaggy, save for a <a href="/wiki/Bob_Hope" title="Bob Hope">Bob Hope</a>-inspired tendency towards temporary bravery.<sup id="cite_ref-RubyAndSpears_7-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-RubyAndSpears-7"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>7<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Later versions of the show made slight changes to the characters' established roles, such as showing the Daphne in 1990s and 2000s <i>Scooby-Doo</i> productions as knowing many forms of <a href="/wiki/Karate" title="Karate">karate</a> and having the ability to defend herself, and reducing her tendency towards being kidnapped.
</p><p><i>Scooby-Doo</i> itself influenced many other Saturday-morning <a href="/wiki/Cartoon" title="Cartoon">cartoons</a> of the 1970s. During that decade, Hanna-Barbera and its rivals produced several animated programs also featuring teenage detectives solving mysteries with a pet or mascot of some sort, including <i><a href="/wiki/Josie_and_the_Pussycats_(TV_series)" title="Josie and the Pussycats (TV series)">Josie and the Pussycats</a></i> (1970–71), <i><a href="/wiki/The_Funky_Phantom" title="The Funky Phantom">The Funky Phantom</a></i> (1971–72), <i><a href="/wiki/The_Amazing_Chan_and_the_Chan_Clan" title="The Amazing Chan and the Chan Clan">The Amazing Chan and the Chan Clan</a></i> (1972–73), <i><a href="/wiki/Speed_Buggy" title="Speed Buggy">Speed Buggy</a></i> (1973–74), <i><a href="/wiki/Goober_and_the_Ghost_Chasers" title="Goober and the Ghost Chasers">Goober and the Ghost Chasers</a></i> (1973–74), <i><a href="/wiki/Jabberjaw" title="Jabberjaw">Jabberjaw</a></i> (1976–78), and <i><a href="/wiki/Captain_Caveman_and_the_Teen_Angels" title="Captain Caveman and the Teen Angels">Captain Caveman and the Teen Angels</a></i> (1977–80).<sup id="cite_ref-Burke_and_Burke-p105-119_20-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Burke_and_Burke-p105-119-20"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>20<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="The_New_Scooby-Doo_Movies"><i>The New Scooby-Doo Movies</i></h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: The New Scooby-Doo Movies"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>In the fall of 1972, new one-hour episodes under the title <i><a href="/wiki/The_New_Scooby-Doo_Movies" title="The New Scooby-Doo Movies">The New Scooby-Doo Movies</a></i> were created; each episode featuring a real or fictitious guest star helping the gang solve mysteries, including characters from other Hanna-Barbera series such as <i><a href="/wiki/Harlem_Globetrotters_(TV_series)" title="Harlem Globetrotters (TV series)">Harlem Globetrotters</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/Josie_and_the_Pussycats_(TV_series)" title="Josie and the Pussycats (TV series)">Josie and the Pussycats</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/Speed_Buggy" title="Speed Buggy">Speed Buggy</a></i>, the comic book characters <a href="/wiki/Batman" title="Batman">Batman</a> and <a href="/wiki/Robin_(character)" title="Robin (character)">Robin</a> (adapted into their own Hanna-Barbera series, <i><a href="/wiki/Super_Friends" title="Super Friends">Super Friends</a></i>, a year later), and celebrities such as <a href="/wiki/Sandy_Duncan" title="Sandy Duncan">Sandy Duncan</a>, <a href="/wiki/The_Addams_Family" title="The Addams Family">The Addams Family</a>, <a href="/wiki/Cass_Elliot" title="Cass Elliot">Cass Elliot</a>, <a href="/wiki/Phyllis_Diller" title="Phyllis Diller">Phyllis Diller</a>, <a href="/wiki/Don_Knotts" title="Don Knotts">Don Knotts</a> and <a href="/wiki/The_Three_Stooges" title="The Three Stooges">The Three Stooges</a>. Hanna-Barbera musical director <a href="/wiki/Hoyt_Curtin" title="Hoyt Curtin">Hoyt Curtin</a> composed a new theme song for this series, and Curtin's theme remained in use for much of <i>Scooby-Doo's</i> original broadcast run. After two seasons and 24 episodes of the <i>New Movies</i> format from 1972 to 1973, CBS began airing reruns of the original <i>Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!</i> series until its option on the series expired in 1976.<sup id="cite_ref-STUEP1_6-8" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-STUEP1-6"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="ABC_years_(1976–91)"><span id="ABC_years_.281976.E2.80.9391.29"></span>ABC years (1976–91)</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: ABC years (1976–91)"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="The_Scooby-Doo_Show_and_Scooby's_All-Star_Laff-A-Lympics"><span id="The_Scooby-Doo_Show_and_Scooby.27s_All-Star_Laff-A-Lympics"></span><i>The Scooby-Doo Show</i> and <i>Scooby's All-Star Laff-A-Lympics</i></h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=6" title="Edit section: The Scooby-Doo Show and Scooby's All-Star Laff-A-Lympics"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>Now president of <a href="/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company" title="American Broadcasting Company">ABC</a>, Fred Silverman made a deal with Hanna-Barbera to bring new episodes of <i>Scooby-Doo</i> to the ABC Saturday-morning lineup, where the show went through almost yearly lineup changes. For their 1976–77 season, 16 new episodes of Scooby-Doo were joined with a new Hanna-Barbera show, <i><a href="/wiki/Dynomutt,_Dog_Wonder" title="Dynomutt, Dog Wonder">Dynomutt, Dog Wonder</a></i>, to create <i><a href="/wiki/The_Scooby-Doo/Dynomutt_Hour" title="The Scooby-Doo/Dynomutt Hour">The Scooby-Doo/Dynomutt Hour</a></i> (the show became <i>The Scooby-Doo/Dynomutt Show</i> when a bonus <i>Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!</i> rerun was added to the package in November 1976). Joe Ruby and Ken Spears, now working for Silverman as supervisors of the ABC Saturday-morning programs, returned the program to its original <i>Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!</i> format, with the addition of Scooby's dim-witted country cousin <a href="/wiki/Scooby-Dum" class="mw-redirect" title="Scooby-Dum">Scooby-Dum</a>, voiced by <a href="/wiki/Daws_Butler" title="Daws Butler">Daws Butler</a>, as a recurring character.<sup id="cite_ref-STUEP1_6-9" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-STUEP1-6"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The voice cast was held over from <i>The New Scooby-Doo Movies</i> save for Nicole Jaffe, who retired from acting in 1973. <a href="/wiki/Pat_Stevens" title="Pat Stevens">Pat Stevens</a> took over her role as the voice of Velma.
</p><p>Then Joe Ruby and Ken Spears left again to start their own studio in 1977 as competition for Hanna-Barbera.<sup id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-21"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>21<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> They would remain away for the rest of the 1980s.
</p><p>For the 1977–78 season, <i>The Scooby-Doo/Dynomutt Show</i> became the two-hour programming block <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby%27s_All-Star_Laff-A-Lympics" title="Scooby's All-Star Laff-A-Lympics">Scooby's All-Star Laff-A-Lympics</a></i> (1977–78) with the addition of <i><a href="/wiki/Laff-a-Lympics" class="mw-redirect" title="Laff-a-Lympics">Laff-a-Lympics</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/Captain_Caveman_and_the_Teen_Angels" title="Captain Caveman and the Teen Angels">Captain Caveman and the Teen Angels</a></i>. In addition to eight new episodes of <i>Scooby-Doo</i> and reruns of the 1969 show, Scooby-Doo also appeared during the <i>All-Star</i> block's <i>Laff-a-Lympics</i> series, which featured 45 Hanna-Barbera characters competing in <i><a href="/wiki/Battle_of_the_Network_Stars" title="Battle of the Network Stars">Battle of the Network Stars</a></i>-esque parodies of <a href="/wiki/Summer_Olympic_Games" title="Summer Olympic Games">Olympic</a> sporting events. Scooby was seen as the team captain of the <i>Laff-a-Lympics</i> "Scooby-Doobies" team, which also featured Shaggy and Scooby-Dum among its members.
</p><p><i>Scooby's All-Star Laff-a-Lympics</i> was retitled <i>Scooby's All Stars</i> for the 1978–79 season, reduced to 90 minutes when <i>Dynomutt</i> was spun off into its own half-hour and the 1969 reruns were dropped. <i>Scooby's All-Stars</i> continued broadcasting reruns of <i>Scooby-Doo</i> from 1976 and 1977, while new episodes of <i>Scooby-Doo</i> aired during a separate half-hour under the <i>Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!</i> banner. After nine weeks, the separate <i>Where Are You!</i> broadcast was cancelled, and the remainder of the 16 new 1978 episodes debuted during the <i>Scooby's All-Stars</i> block.<sup id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-22"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>22<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The 40 total <i>Scooby-Doo</i> episodes produced from 1976 to 1978 were later packaged together for <a href="/wiki/Broadcast_syndication" title="Broadcast syndication">syndication</a> as <i><a href="/wiki/The_Scooby-Doo_Show" title="The Scooby-Doo Show">The Scooby-Doo Show</a></i>, under which title they continue to air.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Scooby-Doo_and_Scrappy-Doo"><i>Scooby-Doo and Scrappy-Doo</i></h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=7" title="Edit section: Scooby-Doo and Scrappy-Doo"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>The <i>Scooby-Doo</i> characters first appeared outside of their regular Saturday-morning format in <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby_Goes_Hollywood" title="Scooby Goes Hollywood">Scooby Goes Hollywood</a></i>, an hour-long ABC <a href="/wiki/Television_special" title="Television special">television special</a> aired in <a href="/wiki/Prime_time" title="Prime time">prime time</a> on December 13, 1979. The special revolved around Shaggy and Scooby attempting to convince the network to move Scooby out of Saturday morning and into a prime-time series, and featured spoofs of then-current television series and films such as <i><a href="/wiki/Happy_Days" title="Happy Days">Happy Days</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/Superman_(1978_film)" title="Superman (1978 film)">Superman: The Movie</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/Laverne_%26_Shirley" title="Laverne & Shirley">Laverne & Shirley</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/Charlie%27s_Angels" title="Charlie's Angels">Charlie's Angels</a></i>.
</p><p>In 1979, Scooby's tiny nephew <a href="/wiki/Scrappy-Doo" title="Scrappy-Doo">Scrappy-Doo</a> was added to both the series and the billing, in an attempt to boost <i>Scooby-Doo</i><span class="nowrap" style="padding-left:0.1em;">'</span>s slipping <a href="/wiki/Nielsen_ratings" class="mw-redirect" title="Nielsen ratings">ratings</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-ScrappyDays_23-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ScrappyDays-23"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>23<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The 1979–80 episodes, aired under the new title <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo_and_Scrappy-Doo_(1979_TV_series)" title="Scooby-Doo and Scrappy-Doo (1979 TV series)">Scooby-Doo and Scrappy-Doo</a></i> as an independent half-hour show, succeeded in regenerating interest in the show. <a href="/wiki/Lennie_Weinrib" title="Lennie Weinrib">Lennie Weinrib</a> voiced Scrappy in the 1979–80 episodes, with Don Messick assuming the role thereafter.<sup id="cite_ref-ScrappyDays_23-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ScrappyDays-23"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>23<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Marla Frumkin replaced Pat Stevens as the voice of Velma mid-season.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Scooby-Doo_and_Scrappy-Doo_shorts"><i>Scooby-Doo and Scrappy-Doo</i> shorts</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=8" title="Edit section: Scooby-Doo and Scrappy-Doo shorts"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>As a result of <i>Scooby-Doo and Scrappy-Doo</i><span class="nowrap" style="padding-left:0.1em;">'s</span> success, the entire show was overhauled in 1980 to focus more upon Scrappy-Doo. At this time, Scooby-Doo started to walk and run anthropomorphically on two feet more often, rather than on four like a normal dog as he did previously. Fred, Daphne, and Velma were dropped from the series, and the <a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo_and_Scrappy-Doo_(1980_TV_series)" title="Scooby-Doo and Scrappy-Doo (1980 TV series)">new <i>Scooby-Doo and Scrappy-Doo</i> format</a> now consisted of three seven-minute comedic adventures starring Scooby, Scrappy, and Shaggy instead of one half-hour mystery. Most of the supernatural villains in the seven-minute <i>Scooby and Scrappy</i> cartoons, who in previous <i>Scooby</i> series had been revealed to be human criminals in <a href="/wiki/Costume" title="Costume">costume</a>, were now real within the context of the series.
</p><p>This version of <i>Scooby-Doo and Scrappy-Doo</i> first aired from 1980 to 1982 as part of <i><a href="/wiki/The_Richie_Rich/Scooby-Doo_Show" title="The Richie Rich/Scooby-Doo Show">The Richie Rich/Scooby-Doo Show</a></i>, an hour-long program also featuring episodes of Hanna-Barbera's new <i><a href="/wiki/Richie_Rich_(1980_TV_series)" title="Richie Rich (1980 TV series)">Richie Rich</a></i> cartoon, adapted from the <a href="/wiki/Harvey_Comics" title="Harvey Comics">Harvey Comics</a> character. From 1982 to 1983, <i>Scooby-Doo and Scrappy-Doo</i> were part of <i><a href="/wiki/The_Scooby-Doo/Scrappy-Doo/Puppy_Hour" class="mw-redirect" title="The Scooby-Doo/Scrappy-Doo/Puppy Hour">The Scooby-Doo/Scrappy-Doo/Puppy Hour</a></i>, a co-production with <a href="/wiki/Ruby-Spears_Productions" class="mw-redirect" title="Ruby-Spears Productions">Ruby-Spears Productions</a> which featured two <i>Scooby and Scrappy</i> shorts, a <i>Scrappy and Yabba-Doo</i> short featuring Scrappy-Doo and his <a href="/wiki/Western_(genre)" title="Western (genre)">Western</a> deputy uncle Yabba-Doo, and <i><a href="/wiki/The_Puppy%27s_New_Adventures" class="mw-redirect" title="The Puppy's New Adventures">The Puppy's New Adventures</a></i>, based on characters from a 1977 Ruby-Spears TV special. Despite the popularity, this was negatively hated by fans for how it dropped the mystery format and other main characters like Fred, Daphne, and Velma.
</p><p>Beginning in 1980, a half-hour of reruns from previous incarnations of <i>Scooby-Doo</i> were broadcast on ABC Saturday mornings in addition to first-run episodes. Airing under the titles <i>Scooby-Doo Classics</i>, <i><a href="/wiki/Scary_Scooby_Funnies" title="Scary Scooby Funnies">Scary Scooby Funnies</a></i>, <i>The Best of Scooby-Doo</i>, and <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby%27s_Mystery_Funhouse" title="Scooby's Mystery Funhouse">Scooby's Mystery Funhouse</a></i>, the rerun package remained on the air until the end of the 1986 season.<sup id="cite_ref-McNeil3_24-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-McNeil3-24"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>24<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="The_New_Scooby_and_Scrappy-Doo_Show"><i>The New Scooby and Scrappy-Doo Show</i></h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=9" title="Edit section: The New Scooby and Scrappy-Doo Show"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p><i>Scooby-Doo</i> was restored to a standalone half-hour in 1983 with <i><a href="/wiki/The_New_Scooby_and_Scrappy-Doo_Show" title="The New Scooby and Scrappy-Doo Show">The New Scooby and Scrappy-Doo Show</a></i> in 1983, which comprised two 11-minute mysteries per episode in a format reminiscent of the original <i>Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!</i> mysteries. Heather North returned to the voice cast as Daphne, who in this incarnation solved mysteries with Shaggy, Scooby, and Scrappy while working undercover as a reporter for a teen magazine.
</p><p>This version of the show lasted for two seasons, with the second season airing under the title <i>The New Scooby-Doo Mysteries</i>. The 1984–85 season episodes featured semi-regular appearances from Fred and Velma, with Frank Welker and Marla Frumkin resuming their respective roles for these episodes.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="The_13_Ghosts_of_Scooby-Doo"><i>The 13 Ghosts of Scooby-Doo</i></h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=10" title="Edit section: The 13 Ghosts of Scooby-Doo"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>1985 saw the debut of <i><a href="/wiki/The_13_Ghosts_of_Scooby-Doo" title="The 13 Ghosts of Scooby-Doo">The 13 Ghosts of Scooby-Doo</a></i>, which featured Daphne, Shaggy, Scooby, Scrappy, and new characters Flim-Flam (voiced by <a href="/wiki/Susan_Blu" title="Susan Blu">Susan Blu</a>)<sup id="cite_ref-TRueggerInterview_25-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-TRueggerInterview-25"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>25<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and Vincent Van Ghoul (based upon and voiced by <a href="/wiki/Vincent_Price" title="Vincent Price">Vincent Price</a>) traveling the globe to capture "thirteen of the most terrifying ghosts upon the face of the earth." The final first-run episode of <i>The 13 Ghosts of Scooby-Doo</i> aired in December 1985, and after its reruns were removed from the ABC lineup the following March, no new <i>Scooby</i> series aired on the network for the next two years.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="A_Pup_Named_Scooby-Doo"><i>A Pup Named Scooby-Doo</i></h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=11" title="Edit section: A Pup Named Scooby-Doo"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>In 1988, after ABC's initiative to shift its Saturday morning block toward preschoolers had spectacularly failed (in part, ABC alleged, due to the introduction of <a href="/wiki/People_meter" title="People meter">people meters</a> that preschoolers were too young to operate), ABC launched an initiative to revive classic properties that older children and parents of younger children would recognize.<sup id="cite_ref-Honey_26-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Honey-26"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>26<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Hanna-Barbera reincarnated the original <i>Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!</i> cast as <a href="/wiki/Elementary_school" class="mw-redirect" title="Elementary school">elementary school</a> students (a common trope in 1980s children's TV) for a new series titled <i><a href="/wiki/A_Pup_Named_Scooby-Doo" title="A Pup Named Scooby-Doo">A Pup Named Scooby-Doo</a></i>, which debuted on ABC in 1988. <i>A Pup Named Scooby-Doo</i> was an irreverent re-imagining of the series, heavily inspired by the classic cartoons of <a href="/wiki/Tex_Avery" title="Tex Avery">Tex Avery</a> and <a href="/wiki/Bob_Clampett" title="Bob Clampett">Bob Clampett</a>, and eschewed the realistic aesthetic of the original <i>Scooby</i> series for a more <i><a href="/wiki/Looney_Tunes" title="Looney Tunes">Looney Tunes</a></i>-like style, including an episode where Scooby-Doo's parents show up and reveal his real name to be "Scoobert". At the same time, the series returned to its original formula in that the group unmasked human villains in costume, as opposed to the supernatural monsters of the early to mid-1980s. The series also established "Coolsville" as the name of the gang's hometown; this setting was retained for several of the later <i>Scooby</i> productions. The retooled show was a success, remaining in production for four seasons and on ABC's lineup until 1991.
</p><p><i>A Pup Named Scooby-Doo</i> was developed and produced by <a href="/wiki/Tom_Ruegger" title="Tom Ruegger">Tom Ruegger</a>, who had been the head <a href="/wiki/Story_editor" title="Story editor">story editor</a> on <i>Scooby-Doo</i> since 1983. Following the first season of <i>A Pup Named Scooby-Doo</i>, Ruegger and much of his unit defected from Hanna-Barbera to <a href="/wiki/Warner_Bros._Animation" title="Warner Bros. Animation">Warner Bros. Animation</a> to develop <i><a href="/wiki/Tiny_Toon_Adventures" title="Tiny Toon Adventures">Steven Spielberg Presents Tiny Toon Adventures</a></i> and later <i><a href="/wiki/Animaniacs" title="Animaniacs">Animaniacs</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/Pinky_and_the_Brain" title="Pinky and the Brain">Pinky and the Brain</a></i>, and <i><a href="/wiki/Freakazoid!" title="Freakazoid!">Freakazoid!</a></i>.<sup id="cite_ref-TRueggerInterview_25-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-TRueggerInterview-25"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>25<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Kids'_WB_years_(2002–08)"><span id="Kids.27_WB_years_.282002.E2.80.9308.29"></span>Kids' WB years (2002–08)</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=12" title="Edit section: Kids' WB years (2002–08)"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="What's_New,_Scooby-Doo?"><span id="What.27s_New.2C_Scooby-Doo.3F"></span><i>What's New, Scooby-Doo?</i></h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=13" title="Edit section: What's New, Scooby-Doo?"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>In 2002, following the successes of the Cartoon Network reruns, the direct to video franchise, and the first feature film, <i>Scooby-Doo</i> returned to Saturday morning for the first time in a decade with <i><a href="/wiki/What%27s_New,_Scooby-Doo%3F" title="What's New, Scooby-Doo?">What's New, Scooby-Doo?</a></i>, which aired on <a href="/wiki/Kids%27_WB" title="Kids' WB">Kids' WB</a> from 2002 until 2006. Produced by Warner Bros. Animation, the show follows the format of the original series but places it in the 21st century, featuring frequent inclusion of modern technology in the 2000s (computers, DVD, the Internet, cell phones) and culture.
</p><p>Beginning with this series, Frank Welker took over as Scooby's voice actor, while continuing to provide the voice of Fred as well. Casey Kasem returned as Shaggy, on the condition that the character be depicted as a vegetarian like Kasem himself.<sup id="cite_ref-KasemVegetarian_27-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-KasemVegetarian-27"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>27<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Grey DeLisle continued to voice Daphne, and former <i><a href="/wiki/The_Facts_of_Life_(TV_series)" title="The Facts of Life (TV series)">Facts of Life</a></i> star <a href="/wiki/Mindy_Cohn" title="Mindy Cohn">Mindy Cohn</a> voiced Velma. The series was produced by <a href="/wiki/Chuck_Sheetz" title="Chuck Sheetz">Chuck Sheetz</a>, who had worked on <i><a href="/wiki/The_Simpsons" title="The Simpsons">The Simpsons</a></i>.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Shaggy_&_Scooby-Doo_Get_a_Clue!"><span id="Shaggy_.26_Scooby-Doo_Get_a_Clue.21"></span><i>Shaggy & Scooby-Doo Get a Clue!</i></h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=14" title="Edit section: Shaggy & Scooby-Doo Get a Clue!"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>In September 2006, a new show entitled <i><a href="/wiki/Shaggy_%26_Scooby-Doo_Get_a_Clue!" title="Shaggy & Scooby-Doo Get a Clue!">Shaggy & Scooby-Doo Get a Clue!</a></i> debuted on <a href="/wiki/The_CW" title="The CW">The CW</a>'s Kids' WB Saturday-morning programming block. In the new premise, Shaggy inherits money and a <a href="/wiki/Mansion" title="Mansion">mansion</a> from an uncle, an inventor who has gone into hiding from villains trying to steal his secret invention. The villains, led by "Dr. Phibes" (based primarily upon <a href="/wiki/Dr._Evil" title="Dr. Evil">Dr. Evil</a> from the <i><a href="/wiki/Austin_Powers_(film_series)" class="mw-redirect" title="Austin Powers (film series)">Austin Powers</a> </i>series, and named after Vincent Price's character from <i><a href="/wiki/The_Abominable_Dr._Phibes" title="The Abominable Dr. Phibes">The Abominable Dr. Phibes</a></i>), then use different schemes to try to get the invention from Shaggy and Scooby, who handle the plots alone. Fred, Daphne, and Velma are normally absent, but do make appearances at times to help. The characters were redesigned and the art style revised for the new series. <a href="/wiki/Scott_Menville" title="Scott Menville">Scott Menville</a> voiced Shaggy in the series, with Casey Kasem appearing as the voice of Shaggy's Uncle Albert. <i>Shaggy & Scooby-Doo Get a Clue!</i> ran for two seasons on The CW.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Cartoon_Network_and_Boomerang_years_(2010–21)"><span id="Cartoon_Network_and_Boomerang_years_.282010.E2.80.9321.29"></span>Cartoon Network and Boomerang years (2010–21)</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=15" title="Edit section: Cartoon Network and Boomerang years (2010–21)"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Scooby-Doo!_Mystery_Incorporated"><span id="Scooby-Doo.21_Mystery_Incorporated"></span><i>Scooby-Doo! Mystery Incorporated</i></h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=16" title="Edit section: Scooby-Doo! Mystery Incorporated"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320">
<p>The next <i>Scooby</i> series, <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo!_Mystery_Incorporated" title="Scooby-Doo! Mystery Incorporated">Scooby-Doo! Mystery Incorporated</a></i>, premiered on <a href="/wiki/Cartoon_Network" title="Cartoon Network">Cartoon Network</a> on April 5, 2010.<sup id="cite_ref-incpremiere_28-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-incpremiere-28"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>28<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The first <i>Scooby</i> series produced for cable television, <i>Mystery Incorporated</i> is a <a href="/wiki/Reboot_(fiction)" title="Reboot (fiction)">reboot</a> of the franchise, re-establishing the characters' relationships, personalities, and locations, and expanding their world to feature their parents, high school, and neighbors. The series also borrowed pieces from many parts of <i>Scooby-Doo's</i> long history, as well as characters and elements of other Hanna-Barbera shows to form its back story and the bases of some of its episodes. <a href="/wiki/Matthew_Lillard" title="Matthew Lillard">Matthew Lillard</a> was brought over from the live-action theatrical series as the new voice of Shaggy, while Welker, Cohn, and DeLisle continued in their respective roles. <a href="/wiki/Patrick_Warburton" title="Patrick Warburton">Patrick Warburton</a>, <a href="/wiki/Linda_Cardellini" title="Linda Cardellini">Linda Cardellini</a>, <a href="/wiki/Lewis_Black" title="Lewis Black">Lewis Black</a>, <a href="/wiki/Vivica_A._Fox" title="Vivica A. Fox">Vivica A. Fox</a>, <a href="/wiki/Gary_Cole" title="Gary Cole">Gary Cole</a>, <a href="/wiki/Udo_Kier" title="Udo Kier">Udo Kier</a>, <a href="/wiki/Tim_Matheson" title="Tim Matheson">Tim Matheson</a>, <a href="/wiki/Tia_Carrere" title="Tia Carrere">Tia Carrere</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Kate_Higgins" title="Kate Higgins">Kate Higgins</a> were added as new semi-regular cast members. Casey Kasem appeared in a recurring role as Shaggy's father, one of his last roles before retiring due to declining health.
</p><p>The series, while still following the basic mystery-solving format of its predecessors, was broadcast as a 52-chapter animated <a href="/wiki/Telenovela" title="Telenovela">televised novel</a> and included elements similar to live-action mystery/adventure shows such as <i><a href="/wiki/Buffy_the_Vampire_Slayer" title="Buffy the Vampire Slayer">Buffy the Vampire Slayer</a></i><sup id="cite_ref-29" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-29"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>29<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and <i><a href="/wiki/Lost_(2004_TV_series)" class="mw-redirect" title="Lost (2004 TV series)">Lost</a>.</i><sup id="cite_ref-30" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-30"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>30<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> An overarching mystery surrounding the gang's hometown of Crystal Cove, California became the series' main <a href="/wiki/Story_arc" title="Story arc">story arc</a>, with pieces to the mystery unfolding episode by episode. Also featured were romantic entanglements and interpersonal conflict between the lead characters. The series ran for 52 episodes over two seasons, with a three-part finale airing across April 4 and 5, 2013—exactly three years from the debut.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Be_Cool,_Scooby-Doo!"><span id="Be_Cool.2C_Scooby-Doo.21"></span><i>Be Cool, Scooby-Doo!</i></h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=17" title="Edit section: Be Cool, Scooby-Doo!"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320">
<p>On March 10, 2014, Cartoon Network announced several new series based on classic cartoons, including a new Scooby-Doo animated series titled <i><a href="/wiki/Be_Cool,_Scooby-Doo!" title="Be Cool, Scooby-Doo!">Be Cool, Scooby-Doo!</a></i>.<sup id="cite_ref-31" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-31"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>31<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The show features the gang "living it up" the summer after the gang's senior year of high school. Along the way, they run into monsters and mayhem.<sup id="cite_ref-bcdb_32-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-bcdb-32"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>32<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The series premiered October 5, 2015 on <a href="/wiki/Cartoon_Network" title="Cartoon Network">Cartoon Network</a><sup id="cite_ref-twitter.com_33-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-twitter.com-33"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>33<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and concluded on March 18, 2018.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Scooby-Doo_and_Guess_Who?"><span id="Scooby-Doo_and_Guess_Who.3F"></span><i>Scooby-Doo and Guess Who?</i></h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=18" title="Edit section: Scooby-Doo and Guess Who?"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320">
<p>The Scooby-Doo series <i>Scooby-Doo and Guess Who?</i> premiered on the <a href="/wiki/Boomerang_(TV_network)#Mobile_app/subscription_service" title="Boomerang (TV network)">Boomerang streaming service and app</a> on June 27, 2019. It ran for two seasons, with the second half of the second season airing on <a href="/wiki/HBO_Max" title="HBO Max">HBO Max</a>. The series features the Mystery Inc. gang teaming up with a variety of guest stars to solve mysteries. Guest stars included <a href="/wiki/Halsey_(singer)" title="Halsey (singer)">Halsey</a>, <a href="/wiki/Sia" title="Sia">Sia</a>, <a href="/wiki/Bill_Nye" title="Bill Nye">Bill Nye</a>, <a href="/wiki/Mark_Hamill" title="Mark Hamill">Mark Hamill</a>, <a href="/wiki/Neil_deGrasse_Tyson" title="Neil deGrasse Tyson">Neil deGrasse Tyson</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ricky_Gervais" title="Ricky Gervais">Ricky Gervais</a>, <a href="/wiki/Kenan_Thompson" title="Kenan Thompson">Kenan Thompson</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Chris_Paul" title="Chris Paul">Chris Paul</a>. The series also includes fictional guest stars, including <a href="/wiki/Steve_Urkel" title="Steve Urkel">Steve Urkel</a> (played by <a href="/wiki/Jaleel_White" title="Jaleel White">Jaleel White</a>), <a href="/wiki/Batman" title="Batman">Batman</a> (played by <a href="/wiki/Kevin_Conroy" title="Kevin Conroy">Kevin Conroy</a>), <a href="/wiki/Wonder_Woman" title="Wonder Woman">Wonder Woman</a> (played by <a href="/wiki/Rachel_Kimsey" title="Rachel Kimsey">Rachel Kimsey</a>), the <a href="/wiki/Flash_(DC_Comics_character)" class="mw-redirect" title="Flash (DC Comics character)">Flash</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Sherlock_Holmes" title="Sherlock Holmes">Sherlock Holmes</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-34" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-34"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>34<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Streaming_era_(2021–present)"><span id="Streaming_era_.282021.E2.80.93present.29"></span>Streaming era (2021–present)</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=19" title="Edit section: Streaming era (2021–present)"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Scooby-Doo_and_Guess_Who?_2"><span id="Scooby-Doo_and_Guess_Who.3F_2"></span><i>Scooby-Doo and Guess Who?</i></h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=20" title="Edit section: Scooby-Doo and Guess Who?"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>The remaining eleven episodes of the second season were released through <a href="/wiki/HBO_Max" title="HBO Max">HBO Max</a> on October 1, 2021.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Velma"><i>Velma</i></h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=21" title="Edit section: Velma"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320">
<p><i>Velma</i> is an adult-oriented animated series that premiered on HBO Max on January 12, 2023.<sup id="cite_ref-35" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-35"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>35<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> It ran for two seasons, and marked the first full original Scooby Doo related show on HBO Max since the previous series <i>Guess Who?</i> was picked up by it at the end of its run (originating on Boomerang). The series is an alternate reality prequel and spinoff to the main franchise, taking place before the formation of Mystery Inc., and does not include Scooby-Doo himself. Unlike in the previous series and films, the main characters (and main voice cast) in <i>Velma</i> are multi-racial.<sup id="cite_ref-36" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-36"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>36<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Untitled_live-action_series">Untitled live-action series</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=22" title="Edit section: Untitled live-action series"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>On April 29, 2024, <i>Deadline</i> reported that a live-action <i>Scooby-Doo!</i> series is in development by <a href="/wiki/Berlanti_Productions" title="Berlanti Productions">Berlanti Productions</a> on <a href="/wiki/Netflix" title="Netflix">Netflix</a>, with <a href="/wiki/Josh_Appelbaum" title="Josh Appelbaum">Josh Appelbaum</a> and <a href="/wiki/Scott_Rosenberg" title="Scott Rosenberg">Scott Rosenberg</a> writing; and <a href="/wiki/Greg_Berlanti" title="Greg Berlanti">Greg Berlanti</a>, <a href="/wiki/Sarah_Schechter_(producer)" title="Sarah Schechter (producer)">Sarah Schechter</a>, Leigh London Redman, <a href="/wiki/Andr%C3%A9_Nemec" title="André Nemec">André Nemec</a>, <a href="/wiki/Jeff_Pinkner" title="Jeff Pinkner">Jeff Pinkner</a>, Jonathan Gabay and Midnight Radio's Adrienne Erickson executive producing.<sup id="cite_ref-37" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-37"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>37<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In March 2025, the series was confirmed to be in production.<sup id="cite_ref-38" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-38"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>38<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-39" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-39"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>39<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-40" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-40"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>40<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The series will consist of eight episodes.<sup id="cite_ref-41" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-41"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>41<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Principal_photography" title="Principal photography">Principal photography</a> is expected to begin in early 2026.<sup id="cite_ref-42" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-42"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>42<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> On December 31, 2025, <a href="/wiki/Frank_Welker" title="Frank Welker">Frank Welker</a> was revealed to be reprising his voice role of <a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo_(character)" title="Scooby-Doo (character)">Scooby-Doo</a> in the series.<sup id="cite_ref-43" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-43"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>43<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Mckenna_Grace" title="Mckenna Grace">Mckenna Grace</a> joined the cast as <a href="/wiki/Daphne_Blake" title="Daphne Blake">Daphne Blake</a> in February 2026, having previously voiced a younger version of the character in <i><a href="/wiki/Scoob!" title="Scoob!">Scoob!</a></i><sup id="cite_ref-44" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-44"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>44<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>  In March 2026, it was announced that Tanner Hagen, <a href="/wiki/Abby_Ryder_Fortson" title="Abby Ryder Fortson">Abby Ryder Fortson</a> and <a href="/wiki/Maxwell_Jenkins" title="Maxwell Jenkins">Maxwell Jenkins</a> will be playing <a href="/wiki/Shaggy_Rogers" title="Shaggy Rogers">Shaggy Rogers</a>, <a href="/wiki/Velma_Dinkley" title="Velma Dinkley">Velma Dinkley</a> and <a href="/wiki/Fred_Jones_(Scooby-Doo)" title="Fred Jones (Scooby-Doo)">Fred Jones</a> respectively.<sup id="cite_ref-45" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-45"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Film_and_rerun_history">Film and rerun history</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=23" title="Edit section: Film and rerun history"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Television_films,_reruns,_and_direct-to-video_films"><span id="Television_films.2C_reruns.2C_and_direct-to-video_films"></span>Television films, reruns, and direct-to-video films</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=24" title="Edit section: Television films, reruns, and direct-to-video films"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>From 1987 to 1988, Hanna-Barbera Productions produced <i><a href="/wiki/Hanna-Barbera_Superstars_10" title="Hanna-Barbera Superstars 10">Hanna-Barbera Superstars 10</a></i>, a series of <a href="/wiki/Broadcast_syndication" title="Broadcast syndication">syndicated</a> <a href="/wiki/Television_film" title="Television film">television films</a> featuring their most popular characters, including <a href="/wiki/Yogi_Bear" title="Yogi Bear">Yogi Bear</a>, <a href="/wiki/Huckleberry_Hound" title="Huckleberry Hound">Huckleberry Hound</a>, <a href="/wiki/The_Flintstones" title="The Flintstones">The Flintstones</a>, and <a href="/wiki/The_Jetsons" title="The Jetsons">The Jetsons</a>. Scooby-Doo, Scrappy-Doo and Shaggy starred in three of these films: <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo_Meets_the_Boo_Brothers" title="Scooby-Doo Meets the Boo Brothers">Scooby-Doo Meets the Boo Brothers</a></i> (1987), <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo_and_the_Ghoul_School" title="Scooby-Doo and the Ghoul School">Scooby-Doo and the Ghoul School</a></i> (1988), and <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo_and_the_Reluctant_Werewolf" class="mw-redirect" title="Scooby-Doo and the Reluctant Werewolf">Scooby-Doo and the Reluctant Werewolf</a></i> (1988). These three films took their tone from the early-1980s <i>Scooby-Doo and Scrappy-Doo</i> entries, and featured the characters encountering actual monsters and ghosts rather than masqueraded people. Scooby-Doo and Shaggy later appeared as the narrators of the television film <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo_in_Arabian_Nights" class="mw-redirect" title="Scooby-Doo in Arabian Nights">Arabian Nights</a></i>, originally broadcast by <a href="/wiki/TBS_(TV_network)" class="mw-redirect" title="TBS (TV network)">TBS</a> in 1994, <a href="/wiki/Don_Messick" title="Don Messick">Don Messick</a>'s final outing as the original voice of Scooby-Doo.
</p><p>Reruns of <i>Scooby-Doo</i> have been in <a href="/wiki/Broadcast_syndication" title="Broadcast syndication">syndication</a> since 1980, and have also been shown on <a href="/wiki/Cable_television" title="Cable television">cable television</a> networks such as <a href="/wiki/TBS_(TV_network)" class="mw-redirect" title="TBS (TV network)">TBS Superstation</a> (until 1989) and <a href="/wiki/USA_Network" title="USA Network">USA Network</a> (as part of the <a href="/wiki/USA_Cartoon_Express" title="USA Cartoon Express">USA Cartoon Express</a> from 1990 to 1994). In 1993, <i>A Pup Named Scooby-Doo</i>, having just recently ended its network run on ABC, began reruns on Cartoon Network. With <a href="/wiki/Turner_Broadcasting" class="mw-redirect" title="Turner Broadcasting">Turner Broadcasting</a> purchasing Hanna-Barbera in 1991, in 1994 the <i>Scooby-Doo</i> franchise became exclusive to the Turner networks: Cartoon Network, TBS Superstation, and <a href="/wiki/Turner_Network_Television" class="mw-redirect" title="Turner Network Television">TNT</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-STUEP10_46-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-STUEP10-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>46<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Television_in_Canada" title="Television in Canada">Canadian</a> network <a href="/wiki/TELETOON_(Canada)" class="mw-redirect" title="TELETOON (Canada)">Teletoon</a> began airing <i>Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!</i> in 1997, with the other <i>Scooby</i> series soon following. When TBS and TNT ended their broadcasts of H-B cartoons in 1998, <i>Scooby-Doo</i> became the exclusive property of both Cartoon Network and sister station <a href="/wiki/Boomerang_(TV_network)" title="Boomerang (TV network)">Boomerang</a>.
</p><p>With <i>Scooby-Doo's</i> restored popularity in reruns on Cartoon Network,<sup id="cite_ref-STUEP10_46-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-STUEP10-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>46<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Warner_Bros._Animation" title="Warner Bros. Animation">Warner Bros. Animation</a> and Hanna-Barbera (by then a subsidiary of <a href="/wiki/Warner_Bros." title="Warner Bros.">Warner Bros.</a> following the merger of <a href="/wiki/Time_Warner" class="mw-redirect" title="Time Warner">Time Warner</a> and Turner Entertainment in 1996) began producing one new <i>Scooby-Doo</i> direct-to-video film a year, beginning in 1998.<sup id="cite_ref-STUEP10_46-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-STUEP10-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>46<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> These films featured a slightly older version of the original five-character cast from the <i>Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!</i> days. The first four DTV entries were <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo_on_Zombie_Island" title="Scooby-Doo on Zombie Island">Scooby-Doo on Zombie Island</a></i> (1998), <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo!_and_the_Witch%27s_Ghost" title="Scooby-Doo! and the Witch's Ghost">Scooby-Doo! and the Witch's Ghost</a></i> (1999), <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo_and_the_Alien_Invaders" title="Scooby-Doo and the Alien Invaders">Scooby-Doo and the Alien Invaders</a></i> (2000), and <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo_and_the_Cyber_Chase" title="Scooby-Doo and the Cyber Chase">Scooby-Doo and the Cyber Chase</a></i> (2001). Frank Welker was the only original voice cast member to return for these productions. Don Messick had died in 1997 and <a href="/wiki/Casey_Kasem" title="Casey Kasem">Casey Kasem</a>, a strict vegetarian, relinquished the role of Shaggy after having to provide the voice for a 1995 <a href="/wiki/Burger_King" title="Burger King">Burger King</a> commercial.<sup id="cite_ref-KasemVegetarian_27-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-KasemVegetarian-27"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>27<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Therefore, <a href="/wiki/Scott_Innes" title="Scott Innes">Scott Innes</a> took over as both Scooby-Doo and Shaggy (<a href="/wiki/Billy_West" title="Billy West">Billy West</a> voiced Shaggy in <i>Scooby-Doo on Zombie Island</i>). <a href="/wiki/B._J._Ward_(actress)" title="B. J. Ward (actress)">B.J. Ward</a> took over as Velma, and <a href="/wiki/Mary_Kay_Bergman" title="Mary Kay Bergman">Mary Kay Bergman</a> voiced Daphne until her death in November 1999, and was replaced by <a href="/wiki/Grey_DeLisle" title="Grey DeLisle">Grey DeLisle</a>.
</p><p>These first four direct-to-video films differed from the original series format by placing the characters in plots with a darker tone and pitting them against actual supernatural forces. <i>Scooby-Doo on Zombie Island</i>, featured the original 1969 gang, reunited after years of being apart, fighting <a href="/wiki/Louisiana_Voodoo" title="Louisiana Voodoo">voodoo</a>-worshiping cat creatures in the <a href="/wiki/Louisiana" title="Louisiana">Louisiana</a> bayou. <i>Scooby-Doo! and the Witch's Ghost</i> featured an author (voice of <a href="/wiki/Tim_Curry" title="Tim Curry">Tim Curry</a>) returning to his <a href="/wiki/Massachusetts" title="Massachusetts">Massachusetts</a> hometown with the gang, to find out that an event is being haunted by the author's dead ancestor Sarah, who was an actual witch. <i>The Witch's Ghost</i> introduced a <a href="/wiki/Goth_rock" class="mw-redirect" title="Goth rock">goth rock</a> band known as The Hex Girls, who became recurring characters in the <i>Scooby-Doo</i> franchise.
</p><p><i>Scooby-Doo and the Cyber Chase</i> was the final production made by the Hanna-Barbera studio, which was absorbed into parent company <a href="/wiki/Warner_Bros._Animation" title="Warner Bros. Animation">Warner Bros. Animation</a> following William Hanna's death in 2001. Warner Animation continued production of the direct-to-video series while also producing new <i>Scooby-Doo</i> series for television.
</p><p>The direct-to-video productions continued to be produced concurrently with at least one entry per year through to 2023. Two of these entries, <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo!_and_the_Legend_of_the_Vampire" title="Scooby-Doo! and the Legend of the Vampire">Scooby-Doo! and the Legend of the Vampire</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo!_and_the_Monster_of_Mexico" title="Scooby-Doo! and the Monster of Mexico">Scooby-Doo! and the Monster of Mexico</a></i> (both 2003) were produced in a retro-style reminiscent of the original series, and featured Heather North and Nicole Jaffe as the voices of Daphne and Velma, respectively. Later entries produced between 2004 and 2009 were done in the style of <i>What's New, Scooby-Doo</i>, using that show's voice cast. Entries from 2010 on use the original 1969 designs and feature Matthew Lillard as the voice of Shaggy, the character Lillard portrayed in the live-action theatrical <i>Scooby-Doo</i> films. Two <i>Scooby-Doo!</i> movies were released in 2016, named <i><a href="/wiki/Lego_Scooby-Doo!_Haunted_Hollywood" title="Lego Scooby-Doo! Haunted Hollywood">Lego Scooby-Doo! Haunted Hollywood</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo!_and_WWE:_Curse_of_the_Speed_Demon" title="Scooby-Doo! and WWE: Curse of the Speed Demon">Scooby-Doo! and WWE: Curse of the Speed Demon</a></i>.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Scooby-Doo!_direct-to-video_specials"><span id="Scooby-Doo.21_direct-to-video_specials"></span><i>Scooby-Doo!</i> direct-to-video specials</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=25" title="Edit section: Scooby-Doo! direct-to-video specials"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>Beginning in 2012, Warner Bros. Animation began producing direct-to-video special episodes in the style of the concurrently produced films for inclusion on <i>Scooby-Doo</i> compilation DVD sets otherwise including episodes from previous Scooby series. These include <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo!_Spooky_Games" class="mw-redirect" title="Scooby-Doo! Spooky Games">Scooby-Doo! Spooky Games</a></i>, included on the July 2012 release <i>Scooby-Doo! Laff-A-Lympics: Spooky Games</i>,<sup id="cite_ref-47" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-47"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>47<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-48" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-48"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>48<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo!_Haunted_Holidays" title="Scooby-Doo! Haunted Holidays">Scooby-Doo! Haunted Holidays</a></i>, from the October 2012 release <i>Scooby-Doo! 13 Spooky Tales: Holiday Chills and Thrills</i>, and <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo!_and_the_Spooky_Scarecrow" class="mw-redirect" title="Scooby-Doo! and the Spooky Scarecrow">Scooby-Doo! and the Spooky Scarecrow</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo!_Mecha_Mutt_Menace" title="Scooby-Doo! Mecha Mutt Menace">Scooby-Doo! Mecha Mutt Menace</a></i>, from the September 2013 DVD releases <i>Scooby-Doo! 13 Spooky Tales: Run for Your 'Rife!</i><sup id="cite_ref-49" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-49"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>49<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and <i>Scooby-Doo! 13 Spooky Tales: Ruh-Roh Robot!</i>.<sup id="cite_ref-50" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-50"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>50<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> On May 13, 2014, another episode, <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo!_Ghastly_Goals" class="mw-redirect" title="Scooby-Doo! Ghastly Goals">Scooby-Doo! Ghastly Goals</a></i> was released on the <i>Scooby-Doo! 13 Spooky Tales: Field of Screams</i> DVD.<sup id="cite_ref-51" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-51"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>51<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> On May 5, 2015, <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo!_and_the_Beach_Beastie" title="Scooby-Doo! and the Beach Beastie">Scooby-Doo! and the Beach Beastie</a></i>, the sixth direct-to-video special, was released on the <i>Scooby-Doo! 13 Spooky Tales: Surf's Up Scooby-Doo</i> DVD.<sup id="cite_ref-moviesunlimited.com_52-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-moviesunlimited.com-52"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>52<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The direct-to-video series' 34th installment, <i><a href="/wiki/Trick_or_Treat_Scooby-Doo!" title="Trick or Treat Scooby-Doo!">Trick or Treat Scooby-Doo!</a></i> (2022), made headlines for portraying Velma as a lesbian (by showing her "crushing big time" on a female guest character), which was in accordance with long-held fan speculation but had never previously been depicted.<sup id="cite_ref-53" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-53"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>53<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Live-action_films">Live-action films</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=26" title="Edit section: Live-action films"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Scooby-doo_logo_movie.webp" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/Scooby-doo_logo_movie.webp/250px-Scooby-doo_logo_movie.webp.png" decoding="async" width="250" height="97" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/Scooby-doo_logo_movie.webp/500px-Scooby-doo_logo_movie.webp.png 2x" data-file-width="800" data-file-height="310"></a><figcaption><i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo_(film)" title="Scooby-Doo (film)">Scooby-Doo</a></i> (2002) logo</figcaption></figure>
<p>A <a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo_(film)" title="Scooby-Doo (film)">feature-length live-action film version</a> of <i>Scooby-Doo</i> was released by <a href="/wiki/Warner_Bros._Pictures" title="Warner Bros. Pictures">Warner Bros. Pictures</a> on June 14, 2002. Directed by <a href="/wiki/Raja_Gosnell" title="Raja Gosnell">Raja Gosnell</a>, the film starred <a href="/wiki/Freddie_Prinze_Jr." title="Freddie Prinze Jr.">Freddie Prinze Jr.</a> as Fred, <a href="/wiki/Sarah_Michelle_Gellar" title="Sarah Michelle Gellar">Sarah Michelle Gellar</a> as Daphne, <a href="/wiki/Matthew_Lillard" title="Matthew Lillard">Matthew Lillard</a> as Shaggy, and <a href="/wiki/Linda_Cardellini" title="Linda Cardellini">Linda Cardellini</a> as Velma. Scooby-Doo, voiced by <a href="/wiki/Neil_Fanning" title="Neil Fanning">Neil Fanning</a>, was created on-screen by <a href="/wiki/Computer-generated_imagery" title="Computer-generated imagery">computer-generated</a> <a href="/wiki/Special_effect" title="Special effect">special effects</a>. <i>Scooby-Doo</i> was a financially successful release, with a domestic box office gross of over US$130 million,<sup id="cite_ref-54" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-54"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>54<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> despite poor reviews from critics.
