</p><p>A sequel, <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo_2:_Monsters_Unleashed" title="Scooby-Doo 2: Monsters Unleashed">Scooby-Doo 2: Monsters Unleashed</a></i>, followed in March 2004 with the same cast and director. <i>Scooby-Doo 2</i> earned US$84 (€55.98) million at the U.S. box office.<sup id="cite_ref-55" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-55"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>55<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> A third film was planned, but later scrapped following Warner Bros.' disappointment at the returns from <i>Scooby-Doo 2</i>.<sup id="cite_ref-56" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-56"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>56<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-57" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-57"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>57<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>In addition, a live-action television film, <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo!_The_Mystery_Begins" title="Scooby-Doo! The Mystery Begins">Scooby-Doo! The Mystery Begins</a></i>, was released on DVD and simultaneously aired on Cartoon Network on September 13, 2009, the 40th anniversary of the series' debut.<sup id="cite_ref-58" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-58"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>58<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The film starred <a href="/wiki/Nick_Palatas" title="Nick Palatas">Nick Palatas</a> as Shaggy, <a href="/wiki/Robbie_Amell" title="Robbie Amell">Robbie Amell</a> as Fred, <a href="/wiki/Kate_Melton" title="Kate Melton">Kate Melton</a> as Daphne, <a href="/wiki/Hayley_Kiyoko" title="Hayley Kiyoko">Hayley Kiyoko</a> as Velma, and Frank Welker as the voice of Scooby-Doo. A second live-action TV movie, <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo!_Curse_of_the_Lake_Monster" title="Scooby-Doo! Curse of the Lake Monster">Scooby-Doo! Curse of the Lake Monster</a></i>, retained the same cast and aired on October 16, 2010, and a direct-to-video spin-off <i><a href="/wiki/Daphne_%26_Velma" title="Daphne & Velma">Daphne & Velma</a></i> in 2018. <i>The Mystery Begins</i><sup id="cite_ref-59" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-59"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>59<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and <i>Curse of the Lake Monster</i> served as a reboot series to the franchise, while <i>Daphne and Velma</i> serves as a spin-off/prequel.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Theatrical_animated_film">Theatrical animated film</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=27" title="Edit section: Theatrical animated film"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320">
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Scoob_Logo.png" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/Scoob_Logo.png/250px-Scoob_Logo.png" decoding="async" width="250" height="105" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/91/Scoob_Logo.png 2x" data-file-width="474" data-file-height="200"></a><figcaption><i><a href="/wiki/Scoob!" title="Scoob!">Scoob!</a></i> (2020) logo</figcaption></figure>
<p>In 2013, Warner Bros. Pictures was developing a fully animated Scooby-Doo feature film with <a href="/wiki/Warner_Animation_Group" class="mw-redirect" title="Warner Animation Group">Warner Animation Group</a>. Charles Roven and Richard Suckle, who produced the first two live-action films, were producing the animated film, and Matt Lieberman was writing the film.<sup id="cite_ref-60" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-60"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>60<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In 2014, Warner Bros. was restarting the film series with Randall Green writing a new movie.<sup id="cite_ref-61" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-61"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>61<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-62" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-62"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>62<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In 2015, Warner Bros. had <a href="/wiki/Tony_Cervone" class="mw-redirect" title="Tony Cervone">Tony Cervone</a> lined up to direct an animated film, with <a href="/wiki/Allison_Abbate" title="Allison Abbate">Allison Abbate</a> as producer and <a href="/wiki/Dan_Povenmire" title="Dan Povenmire">Dan Povenmire</a> as executive producer. Originally planned for a September 21, 2018 release, it was later pushed back to May 15, 2020, with <a href="/wiki/Dax_Shepard" title="Dax Shepard">Dax Shepard</a> co-directing and co-writing.<sup id="cite_ref-63" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-63"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>63<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-64" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-64"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>64<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-slashfilm.com_65-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-slashfilm.com-65"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>65<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The Hollywood Reporter announced that Frank Welker will be reprising his voice role as Scooby, and that he will be joined by <a href="/wiki/Will_Forte" title="Will Forte">Will Forte</a> and <a href="/wiki/Gina_Rodriguez" title="Gina Rodriguez">Gina Rodriguez</a> voicing Shaggy and Velma, while <a href="/wiki/Tracy_Morgan" title="Tracy Morgan">Tracy Morgan</a> will be voicing Captain Caveman, from the Hanna-Barbera series <i><a href="/wiki/Captain_Caveman_and_the_Teen_Angels" title="Captain Caveman and the Teen Angels">Captain Caveman and the Teen Angels</a></i> and Deadline reported that <a href="/wiki/Zac_Efron" title="Zac Efron">Zac Efron</a> and <a href="/wiki/Amanda_Seyfried" title="Amanda Seyfried">Amanda Seyfried</a> will voice Fred and Daphne. In addition, <a href="/wiki/Ken_Jeong" title="Ken Jeong">Ken Jeong</a> will be voicing <a href="/wiki/Dynomutt,_Dog_Wonder" title="Dynomutt, Dog Wonder">Dynomutt, Dog Wonder</a> from Hanna-Barbera series of the same name and <a href="/wiki/Kiersey_Clemons" title="Kiersey Clemons">Kiersey Clemons</a> will voice Dee Dee Skyes, a character from Captain Caveman and the Teen Angels.<sup id="cite_ref-AnimatedFilmCast_66-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-AnimatedFilmCast-66"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>66<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-67" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-67"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>67<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-68" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-68"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>68<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Blue_Falcon" class="mw-redirect" title="Blue Falcon">Blue Falcon</a>, from <i>Dynomutt, Dog Wonder</i> voiced by <a href="/wiki/Mark_Wahlberg" title="Mark Wahlberg">Mark Wahlberg</a> and <a href="/wiki/Dick_Dastardly" title="Dick Dastardly">Dick Dastardly</a>, from Hanna-Barbera's <i><a href="/wiki/Wacky_Races_(1968_TV_series)" title="Wacky Races (1968 TV series)">Wacky Races</a></i>, will be the film's main antagonist, voiced by <a href="/wiki/Jason_Isaacs" title="Jason Isaacs">Jason Isaacs</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-AnimatedFilmCast_66-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-AnimatedFilmCast-66"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>66<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In March 2020, the film's theatrical release was delayed indefinitely due to the <a href="/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic" title="COVID-19 pandemic">COVID-19 pandemic</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-ScoobDelay_69-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ScoobDelay-69"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>69<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> On April 22, 2020, Warner Bros. announced that due to <a href="/wiki/Impact_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_on_cinema" title="Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on cinema">movie theater closures</a> the theatrical release for <i>Scoob!</i> had been cancelled, with the film released instead on <a href="/wiki/Video_on_demand" title="Video on demand">Premium video on demand</a> in the United States and Canada on May 15, 2020, the original date of release.<sup id="cite_ref-70" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-70"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>70<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In July 2020, class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The film subsequently received a secondary theatrical release in the United States beginning on May 21, 2021, in selected markets.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Cast">Cast</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=28" title="Edit section: Cast"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320">
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Scooby-gang-1969.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/9a/Scooby-gang-1969.jpg/250px-Scooby-gang-1969.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="192" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/9/9a/Scooby-gang-1969.jpg 2x" data-file-width="355" data-file-height="272"></a><figcaption>A scene from "What a Night for a Knight", the first episode of <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo,_Where_Are_You!" title="Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!">Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!</a></i>. Clockwise from top: <a href="/wiki/Shaggy_Rogers" title="Shaggy Rogers">Shaggy Rogers</a>, <a href="/wiki/Fred_Jones_(Scooby-Doo)" title="Fred Jones (Scooby-Doo)">Fred Jones</a>, <a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo_(character)" title="Scooby-Doo (character)">Scooby-Doo</a>, <a href="/wiki/Velma_Dinkley" title="Velma Dinkley">Velma Dinkley</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Daphne_Blake" title="Daphne Blake">Daphne Blake</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<ul><li><b><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo_(character)" title="Scooby-Doo (character)">Scooby-Doo</a></b>: <a href="/wiki/Don_Messick" title="Don Messick">Don Messick</a> was the original voice of Scooby-Doo from 1969 until 1995. <a href="/wiki/Hadley_Kay" title="Hadley Kay">Hadley Kay</a> performed the voice for the <i><a href="/wiki/Johnny_Bravo" title="Johnny Bravo">Johnny Bravo</a></i> episodes "Bravo Dooby-Doo" and "'Twas the Night", as well as in commercials, in 1997. <a href="/wiki/Scott_Innes" title="Scott Innes">Scott Innes</a> was the voice of Scooby-Doo from 1998 to 2002. <a href="/wiki/Neil_Fanning" title="Neil Fanning">Neil Fanning</a> voiced Scooby-Doo in the live-action Warner Bros. theatrical films produced in 2002 and 2004. <a href="/wiki/Frank_Welker" title="Frank Welker">Frank Welker</a> is the current voice of Scooby-Doo, having taken over the role from Innes in 2002, although Innes voiced the character in video game projects (including PC, DVD and board games), commercials and some toys until 2008. <a href="/wiki/Dave_Coulier" title="Dave Coulier">Dave Coulier</a> (2005) and <a href="/wiki/Seth_Green" title="Seth Green">Seth Green</a> (2007, 2012, 2018) voiced Scooby in the <i><a href="/wiki/Robot_Chicken" title="Robot Chicken">Robot Chicken</a></i> parodies.</li>
<li><b><a href="/wiki/Shaggy_Rogers" title="Shaggy Rogers">Norville "Shaggy" Rogers</a></b>: <a href="/wiki/Casey_Kasem" title="Casey Kasem">Casey Kasem</a> was the original voice of Shaggy from 1969 until 1997. <a href="/wiki/Billy_West" title="Billy West">Billy West</a> voiced Shaggy in <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo_on_Zombie_Island" title="Scooby-Doo on Zombie Island">Scooby-Doo on Zombie Island</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo:_Behind_the_Scenes" class="mw-redirect" title="Scooby-Doo: Behind the Scenes">Scooby-Doo: Behind the Scenes</a></i> in 1998. <a href="/wiki/Scott_Innes" title="Scott Innes">Scott Innes</a> voiced the character from 1999 to 2002 and he continued to voice Shaggy in video game projects (including PC, DVD and board games), commercials and some toys until 2009. Casey Kasem returned to the voice role in 2002 and continued as Shaggy until 2009. In 2006, Kasem continued to voice Shaggy only in the direct-to-video film series until 2009, while <a href="/wiki/Scott_Menville" title="Scott Menville">Scott Menville</a> performed the voice of Shaggy in the 2006–08 CW series <i><a href="/wiki/Shaggy_%26_Scooby-Doo_Get_a_Clue!" title="Shaggy & Scooby-Doo Get a Clue!">Shaggy & Scooby-Doo Get a Clue!</a></i>. <a href="/wiki/Matthew_Lillard" title="Matthew Lillard">Matthew Lillard</a> appeared as Shaggy in the live action 2002 and 2004 theatrical films, and took over as the voice of the animated character in 2010. He also voiced Shaggy in four stop-motion parody sketches for the <a href="/wiki/Adult_Swim" title="Adult Swim">Adult Swim</a> show <i><a href="/wiki/Robot_Chicken" title="Robot Chicken">Robot Chicken</a></i>. <a href="/wiki/Nick_Palatas" title="Nick Palatas">Nick Palatas</a> appeared as Shaggy in the 2009 and 2010 live-action TV movies. <a href="/wiki/Will_Forte" title="Will Forte">Will Forte</a> voices Shaggy as an adult with <a href="/wiki/Iain_Armitage" title="Iain Armitage">Iain Armitage</a> voicing his younger self in the theatrical animated film <i><a href="/wiki/Scoob!" title="Scoob!">Scoob!</a></i>.</li>
<li><b><a href="/wiki/Fred_Jones_(Scooby-Doo)" title="Fred Jones (Scooby-Doo)">Fred Jones</a></b>: <a href="/wiki/Frank_Welker" title="Frank Welker">Frank Welker</a> has always performed the voice of the animated versions of Fred since 1969, with the exception of the 1988–91 ABC series <i><a href="/wiki/A_Pup_Named_Scooby-Doo" title="A Pup Named Scooby-Doo">A Pup Named Scooby-Doo</a></i>, where <a href="/wiki/Carl_Steven" title="Carl Steven">Carl Steven</a> performed the voice of preteen Fred. <a href="/wiki/Freddie_Prinze_Jr." title="Freddie Prinze Jr.">Freddie Prinze Jr.</a> appears as Fred in the live-action theatrical films and voiced the character in the <i>Robot Chicken</i> parodies. <a href="/wiki/Robbie_Amell" title="Robbie Amell">Robbie Amell</a> played Fred in the live-action TV movies. <a href="/wiki/Zac_Efron" title="Zac Efron">Zac Efron</a> voices Fred as an adult with <a href="/wiki/Pierce_Gagnon" title="Pierce Gagnon">Pierce Gagnon</a> voicing his younger self in the theatrical animated film <i><a href="/wiki/Scoob!" title="Scoob!">Scoob!</a></i>.</li>
<li><b><a href="/wiki/Daphne_Blake" title="Daphne Blake">Daphne Blake</a></b>: <a href="/wiki/Indira_Stefanianna" title="Indira Stefanianna">Stefanianna Christopherson</a> was the voice of Daphne in the first season of <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo,_Where_Are_You!" title="Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!">Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!</a></i> in 1969–70. <a href="/wiki/Heather_North" title="Heather North">Heather North</a> assumed the role for season two in 1970, and continued as Daphne through 1997, save for <a href="/wiki/Kellie_Martin" title="Kellie Martin">Kellie Martin</a>'s turn as preteen Daphne in <i><a href="/wiki/A_Pup_Named_Scooby-Doo" title="A Pup Named Scooby-Doo">A Pup Named Scooby-Doo</a></i>. <a href="/wiki/Mary_Kay_Bergman" title="Mary Kay Bergman">Mary Kay Bergman</a> performed the voice of Daphne from 1998 to 2000, with <a href="/wiki/Grey_DeLisle" title="Grey DeLisle">Grey DeLisle</a> assuming the role. She continues to perform the role to this day. North reprised her voice role for two 2003 direct-to-video films, <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo!_and_the_Legend_of_the_Vampire" title="Scooby-Doo! and the Legend of the Vampire">Scooby-Doo! and the Legend of the Vampire</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo!_and_the_Monster_of_Mexico" title="Scooby-Doo! and the Monster of Mexico">Scooby-Doo! and the Monster of Mexico</a></i>. <a href="/wiki/Sarah_Michelle_Gellar" title="Sarah Michelle Gellar">Sarah Michelle Gellar</a> appears as Daphne in the live-action theatrical films and as Daphne's voice in the <i>Robot Chicken</i> parodies. <a href="/wiki/Kate_Melton" title="Kate Melton">Kate Melton</a> played Daphne in the live-action TV movies. <a href="/wiki/Amanda_Seyfried" title="Amanda Seyfried">Amanda Seyfried</a> voices Daphne as an adult with <a href="/wiki/Mckenna_Grace" title="Mckenna Grace">Mckenna Grace</a> voicing her younger self in the theatrical animated film <i><a href="/wiki/Scoob!" title="Scoob!">Scoob!</a></i>.</li>
<li><b><a href="/wiki/Velma_Dinkley" title="Velma Dinkley">Velma Dinkley</a></b>: <a href="/wiki/Nicole_Jaffe" title="Nicole Jaffe">Nicole Jaffe</a> was the original voice of Velma from 1969 to 1973. <a href="/wiki/Pat_Stevens" title="Pat Stevens">Pat Stevens</a> assumed the role from 1976 to 1979, with Marla Frumkin taking over midseason on <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo_and_Scrappy-Doo_(1979_TV_series)" title="Scooby-Doo and Scrappy-Doo (1979 TV series)">Scooby-Doo and Scrappy-Doo</a></i> in the latter year. Frumkin returned to voice Velma on a recurring basis for <i><a href="/wiki/The_New_Scooby-Doo_Mysteries" class="mw-redirect" title="The New Scooby-Doo Mysteries">The New Scooby-Doo Mysteries</a></i> in 1984, and Christina Lange voiced preteen Velma in <i><a href="/wiki/A_Pup_Named_Scooby-Doo" title="A Pup Named Scooby-Doo">A Pup Named Scooby-Doo</a></i>. <a href="/wiki/B._J._Ward_(actress)" title="B. J. Ward (actress)">B. J. Ward</a> voiced Velma from 1997 to 2002, with <a href="/wiki/Mindy_Cohn" title="Mindy Cohn">Mindy Cohn</a> assuming the role in 2002. As with North, Jaffe reprised her voice role for <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo!_and_the_Legend_of_the_Vampire" title="Scooby-Doo! and the Legend of the Vampire">Scooby-Doo! and the Legend of the Vampire</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo!_and_the_Monster_of_Mexico" title="Scooby-Doo! and the Monster of Mexico">Scooby-Doo! and the Monster of Mexico</a></i> in 2003. <a href="/wiki/Stephanie_D%27Abruzzo" title="Stephanie D'Abruzzo">Stephanie D'Abruzzo</a> voiced Velma for the 2013 puppet film <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo!_Adventures:_The_Mystery_Map" title="Scooby-Doo! Adventures: The Mystery Map">Scooby-Doo! Adventures: The Mystery Map</a></i>. In 2015, <a href="/wiki/Kate_Micucci" title="Kate Micucci">Kate Micucci</a> took on the role for the series <i><a href="/wiki/Be_Cool,_Scooby-Doo!" title="Be Cool, Scooby-Doo!">Be Cool, Scooby-Doo!</a></i> and Lego Scooby-Doo shorts and specials; in 2016 she took over the role from Cohn completely.<sup id="cite_ref-73" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-73"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>73<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-74" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-74"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>74<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Linda_Cardellini" title="Linda Cardellini">Linda Cardellini</a> appears as Velma in the live-action theatrical films and as the voice of Velma in the <i>Robot Chicken</i> parodies. <a href="/wiki/Hayley_Kiyoko" title="Hayley Kiyoko">Hayley Kiyoko</a> played Velma in the live-action TV movies. <a href="/wiki/Gina_Rodriguez" title="Gina Rodriguez">Gina Rodriguez</a> voices Velma as an adult with <a href="/wiki/Ariana_Greenblatt" title="Ariana Greenblatt">Ariana Greenblatt</a> voicing her younger self in the theatrical animated film <i><a href="/wiki/Scoob!" title="Scoob!">Scoob!</a></i>.</li>
<li><b><a href="/wiki/Scrappy-Doo" title="Scrappy-Doo">Scrappy-Doo</a></b>: <a href="/wiki/Lennie_Weinrib" title="Lennie Weinrib">Lennie Weinrib</a> voiced Scrappy-Doo during the first version of <i>Scooby-Doo and Scrappy-Doo</i> in 1979–80. <a href="/wiki/Don_Messick" title="Don Messick">Don Messick</a> assumed the role in 1980 for the <i>Scooby-Doo and Scrappy-Doo</i> segments of <i><a href="/wiki/The_Richie_Rich/Scooby-Doo_Show" title="The Richie Rich/Scooby-Doo Show">The Richie Rich/Scooby-Doo Show</a></i> and continued as Scrappy through 1988. Scrappy has only appeared sporadically since 1988, with <a href="/wiki/Scott_Innes" title="Scott Innes">Scott Innes</a> performing the voice in the 2002 live-action film, which portrays Scrappy as the main villain, as well as in Cartoon Network bumpers, video games and toys since 1999. <a href="/wiki/Dan_Milano" title="Dan Milano">Dan Milano</a> voiced Scrappy in a 2007 <i>Robot Chicken</i> sketch.</li></ul>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Comic_books">Comic books</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=29" title="Edit section: Comic books"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Mystery_Machine_van.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/3/3a/Mystery_Machine_van.jpg/250px-Mystery_Machine_van.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="187" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/3/3a/Mystery_Machine_van.jpg 2x" data-file-width="352" data-file-height="264"></a><figcaption>A 1968 Chevrolet Sportvan 108 painted to look like The Mystery Machine from <i>Scooby-Doo</i>. A number of <i>Scooby</i> fans have decorated vans in this fashion.</figcaption></figure>
<p><a href="/wiki/Gold_Key_Comics" title="Gold Key Comics">Gold Key Comics</a> began publication of <i>Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!</i> <a href="/wiki/Comic_book" title="Comic book">comic books</a> in March 1970. The comics initially contained adaptations of episodes of the television show drawn by <a href="/wiki/Phil_DeLara" title="Phil DeLara">Phil DeLara</a>, Jack Manning and <a href="/wiki/Warren_Tufts" title="Warren Tufts">Warren Tufts</a>. The comic books later moved to all-original stories until ending with issue #30 in 1974.<sup id="cite_ref-75" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-75"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>75<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Several of these issues were written by <a href="/wiki/Mark_Evanier" title="Mark Evanier">Mark Evanier</a> and drawn by <a href="/wiki/Dan_Spiegle" title="Dan Spiegle">Dan Spiegle</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-ScrappyDays_23-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ScrappyDays-23"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>23<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-ScoobyComics_76-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ScoobyComics-76"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>76<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Charlton_Comics" title="Charlton Comics">Charlton</a> published <i>Scooby</i> comics, many drawn by Bill Williams, for 11 issues in 1975. From 1977 to 1979, <a href="/wiki/Marvel_Comics" title="Marvel Comics">Marvel Comics</a> published nine issues of <i>Scooby-Doo</i>, all written by Evanier and drawn by Spiegel. <a href="/wiki/Harvey_Comics" title="Harvey Comics">Harvey Comics</a> published reprints of the Charlton comics, as well as a handful of special issues, between 1993 and 1994.
</p><p>In 1995, <a href="/wiki/Archie_Comics" title="Archie Comics">Archie Comics</a> began publishing a monthly <i>Scooby-Doo</i> comic book, the first year of which featured Scrappy-Doo among its cast. Evanier and Spiegel worked on three issues of the series, which ended after 21 issues in 1997 when Warner Bros.' <a href="/wiki/DC_Comics" title="DC Comics">DC Comics</a> acquired the rights to publish comics based on Hanna-Barbera characters. DC's <i>Scooby-Doo</i> series continues publication to this day. In 2013, DC began a digital bi-monthly comic book titled <i>Scooby-Doo Team-Up</i>, <a href="/wiki/Crossover_(fiction)" title="Crossover (fiction)">crossing over</a> Mystery Inc. with other DC and Hanna-Barbera characters. Since then, the series has become a monthly comic book available in print.
</p><p>In 2004, a limited series of a 100 comic books called <i>Scooby-Doo! World of Mystery</i> was released. In each issue, Mystery Inc. go from country to country solving mysteries. Each issue came with a pack of exclusive cards, with 350 in total able to be collected.<sup id="cite_ref-77" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-77"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>77<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>In 2016, DC launched a new monthly comic book entitled <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby_Apocalypse" title="Scooby Apocalypse">Scooby Apocalypse</a></i>, with the characters being reinvented in a story set in a <a href="/wiki/Post-apocalyptic_world" class="mw-redirect" title="Post-apocalyptic world">post-apocalyptic world</a>, where monsters roam the streets and Scooby and the gang must find a way to survive at all costs, while also trying to find a way to reverse the apocalypse.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Merchandising">Merchandising</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=30" title="Edit section: Merchandising"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>Early <i>Scooby-Doo</i> merchandise included a 1973 <a href="/wiki/Milton_Bradley_Company" title="Milton Bradley Company">Milton Bradley</a> <a href="/wiki/Board_game" title="Board game">board game</a>, decorated <a href="/wiki/Lunch_box" class="mw-redirect" title="Lunch box">lunch boxes</a>, iron-on transfers, <a href="/wiki/Coloring_book" title="Coloring book">coloring books</a>, story books, <a href="/wiki/Gramophone_record" class="mw-redirect" title="Gramophone record">records</a>, underwear, and other such goods.<sup id="cite_ref-wingnuttoons_78-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-wingnuttoons-78"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>78<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> When Scrappy-Doo was introduced to the series in 1979, he, Scooby, and Shaggy became the foci of much of the merchandising, including a 1983 Milton-Bradley <i>Scooby-Doo and Scrappy-Doo</i> board game. The first <i>Scooby-Doo</i> video game appeared in <a href="/wiki/Arcade_game" title="Arcade game">arcades</a> in 1986, and has been followed by a number of games for both home consoles and personal computers. <i>Scooby-Doo </i><a href="/wiki/Multivitamin" title="Multivitamin">multivitamins</a> also debuted at this time, and have been manufactured by <a href="/wiki/Bayer" title="Bayer">Bayer</a> since 2001.
<i>Scooby-Doo</i> merchandising tapered off during the late 1980s and early 1990s, but increased after the series' revival on Cartoon Network in 1995. Today, all manner of <i>Scooby-Doo</i>-branded products are available for purchase, including <i>Scooby-Doo</i> <a href="/wiki/Breakfast_cereal" title="Breakfast cereal">breakfast cereal</a>, <a href="/wiki/Stuffed_animal" class="mw-redirect" title="Stuffed animal">plush toys</a>, <a href="/wiki/Action_figure" title="Action figure">action figures</a>, car decorations, <a href="/wiki/Barbie" title="Barbie">Barbie</a> dolls from <a href="/wiki/Mattel" title="Mattel">Mattel</a> and much more. Real "Scooby Snacks" <a href="/wiki/Dog_food" title="Dog food">dog treats</a> are produced by Del Monte Pet Products. <a href="/wiki/Hasbro" title="Hasbro">Hasbro</a> has created a number of <i>Scooby</i> board games, including a <i>Scooby</i>-themed edition of the popular mystery board game <i><a href="/wiki/Cluedo" title="Cluedo">Clue</a></i>. In 2007, the <a href="/wiki/Pressman_Toy_Corporation" title="Pressman Toy Corporation">Pressman Toy Corporation</a> released the board game <i>Scooby-Doo! Haunted House</i>. Beginning in 2001, a <i>Scooby-Doo</i> children's book series was authorized and published by <a href="/wiki/Scholastic_Corporation" title="Scholastic Corporation">Scholastic</a>. These books, written by <a href="/wiki/Suzanne_Weyn" title="Suzanne Weyn">Suzanne Weyn</a>, include original stories and adaptations of <i>Scooby</i> theatrical and direct-to-video features.
</p><p>From 1990 to 2002, Shaggy and Scooby-Doo appeared as characters in the <i><a href="/wiki/The_Funtastic_World_of_Hanna-Barbera_(ride)" title="The Funtastic World of Hanna-Barbera (ride)">Funtastic World of Hanna-Barbera</a></i> simulator ride at <a href="/wiki/Universal_Studios_Florida" title="Universal Studios Florida">Universal Studios Florida</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Stokes_79-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Stokes-79"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>79<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The ride was replaced in the early 2000s with a <i><a href="/wiki/Jimmy_Neutron" title="Jimmy Neutron">Jimmy Neutron</a></i> attraction, and <i>The Funtastic World of Hanna-Barbera</i> instead became an attraction at several properties operated by <a href="/wiki/Paramount_Parks" title="Paramount Parks">Paramount Parks</a>. Shaggy and Scooby-Doo are currently <a href="/wiki/Costumed_character" class="mw-redirect" title="Costumed character">costumed characters</a> at Universal Studios Florida, and can be seen driving the Mystery Machine around the park.
</p><p>In 2001, <i>Scooby-Doo in Stagefright</i>, a live stage play based upon the series, began touring across the world. A follow-up, <i>Scooby-Doo and the Pirate Ghost</i>, followed in 2009.
</p><p>The Mystery Machine has been used as the basis for many die-cast models and toys, such as from <a href="/wiki/Hot_Wheels" title="Hot Wheels">Hot Wheels</a>.
</p><p>The brand made $800 million in retail sales in 1999.<sup id="cite_ref-80" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-80"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>80<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-81" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-81"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>81<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In 2004, <i>Scooby-Doo</i> merchandise had generated <span style="white-space: nowrap">$1 billion</span> in retail sales<sup id="cite_ref-82" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-82"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>82<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Licensed merchandise also sold <span style="white-space: nowrap">$496 million</span> in 2015,<sup id="cite_ref-thelicensingletter_83-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-thelicensingletter-83"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>83<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <span style="white-space: nowrap">$501 million</span> in 2016, and <span style="white-space: nowrap">$353 million</span> in 2017.<sup id="cite_ref-tll2017_84-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-tll2017-84"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>84<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>

<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Reception_and_legacy">Reception and legacy</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=33" title="Edit section: Reception and legacy"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:The_Mystery_Machine.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/The_Mystery_Machine.jpg/250px-The_Mystery_Machine.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="140" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/The_Mystery_Machine.jpg/500px-The_Mystery_Machine.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3872" data-file-height="2176"></a><figcaption>The Mystery Machine at <a href="/wiki/San_Diego_Comic-Con" title="San Diego Comic-Con">San Diego Comic-Con</a> in 2013</figcaption></figure>
<p>During its five-decade broadcast history, <i>Scooby-Doo</i> has received two <a href="/wiki/Emmy_Award" class="mw-redirect" title="Emmy Award">Emmy</a> nominations: a 1989 <a href="/wiki/Daytime_Emmy_Award" class="mw-redirect" title="Daytime Emmy Award">Daytime Emmy</a> nomination for <i><a href="/wiki/A_Pup_Named_Scooby-Doo" title="A Pup Named Scooby-Doo">A Pup Named Scooby-Doo</a></i>, and a 2003 Daytime Emmy nomination for <i>What's New, Scooby-Doo</i><span class="nowrap" style="padding-left:0.1em;">'</span>s Mindy Cohn in the "Outstanding Performer in an Animated Program" category.<sup id="cite_ref-awards_at_IMDb_87-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-awards_at_IMDb-87"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>87<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Science advocate <a href="/wiki/Carl_Sagan" title="Carl Sagan">Carl Sagan</a> favorably compared the predominantly skeptic oriented formula to that of most television dealing with paranormal themes, and considered that an adult analogue to <i>Scooby-Doo</i> would be a great public service.<sup id="cite_ref-Sagan_88-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Sagan-88"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>88<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p><i>Scooby-Doo</i> has maintained a significant fan base, which has grown steadily since the 1990s due to the show's popularity among both young children and nostalgic adults who grew up with the series.<sup id="cite_ref-89" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-89"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>89<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Several television critics have stated that the show's mix of the comedy-adventure and horror genres was the reason for its widespread success.<sup id="cite_ref-Elias_90-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Elias-90"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>90<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> As Fred Silverman and the Hanna-Barbera staff had planned when they first began producing the series, <i>Scooby-Doo</i><span class="nowrap" style="padding-left:0.1em;">'</span>s ghosts, monsters and spooky locales tend more towards humor than horror, making them easily accessible to younger children. "Overall, [<i>Scooby-Doo</i> is] just not a show that is going to overstimulate kids' emotions and tensions," offered American Center for Children and Media executive director David Kleeman in a 2002 interview. "It creates just enough fun to make it fun without getting them worried or giving them nightmares.<sup id="cite_ref-filmfreakcentral_91-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-filmfreakcentral-91"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>91<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Older teenagers and adults have admitted to enjoying <i>Scooby-Doo</i> because of presumed subversive themes which involve theories of drug use and sexuality, in particular that Shaggy is assumed to be a user of <a href="/wiki/Cannabis_(drug)" title="Cannabis (drug)">cannabis</a> and Velma is assumed to be a lesbian.<sup id="cite_ref-92" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-92"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>92<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-93" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-93"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>93<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-sdChiTrib_94-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-sdChiTrib-94"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>94<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Such themes were pervasive enough in popular culture to find their way into Warner Bros.' initial <i>Scooby-Doo</i> feature film in 2002,<sup id="cite_ref-sdChiTrib_94-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-sdChiTrib-94"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>94<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-APsdmovie_95-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-APsdmovie-95"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>95<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> though several of the scenes were edited before release to secure a family-friendly <a href="/wiki/Motion_Picture_Association_of_America_film_rating_system" class="mw-redirect" title="Motion Picture Association of America film rating system">"PG"</a> rating.<sup id="cite_ref-APsdmovie_95-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-APsdmovie-95"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>95<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Series creators Joe Ruby and Ken Spears reported that they "took umbrage" to the inclusion of such themes in the <i>Scooby-Doo</i> feature and other places, and denied intending their characters to be drug users in any way.<sup id="cite_ref-STUEP1_6-10" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-STUEP1-6"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Like many Hanna-Barbera shows, the early <i>Scooby-Doo</i> series have been criticized at times for their production values and storytelling.<sup id="cite_ref-96" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-96"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>96<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In 2002, Jamie Malanowski of <i>The New York Times</i> commented that "[<i>Scooby-Doo</i><span class="nowrap" style="padding-left:0.1em;">'</span>s] mysteries are not very mysterious, and the humor is hardly humorous. As for the animation—well, the drawings on your refrigerator may give it competition."<sup id="cite_ref-97" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-97"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>97<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>By the 2000s, <i>Scooby-Doo</i> had received recognition for its popularity by placing in a number of top cartoon or top cartoon character polls. The August 3, 2002, issue of <i><a href="/wiki/TV_Guide" title="TV Guide">TV Guide</a></i> featured its list of the 50 Greatest Cartoon Characters of All Time, in which Scooby-Doo placed twenty-second.<sup id="cite_ref-50_Greatest_98-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-50_Greatest-98"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>98<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Scooby also ranked thirteenth in <a href="/wiki/Animal_Planet" title="Animal Planet">Animal Planet</a>'s list of the 50 Greatest TV Animals.<sup id="cite_ref-50_TV_Animals_99-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-50_TV_Animals-99"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>99<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> For one year from 2004 to 2005, <i>Scooby-Doo</i> held the <a href="/wiki/Guinness_World_Records" title="Guinness World Records">Guinness World Record</a> for having the most episodes of any animated television series ever produced, a record previously held by and later returned to <i><a href="/wiki/The_Simpsons" title="The Simpsons">The Simpsons</a></i>. <i>Scooby-Doo</i> was published as holding this record in the 2006 edition of the <i>Guinness Book of Records</i>.<sup id="cite_ref-bbc_100-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-bbc-100"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>100<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>In January 2009, entertainment website <a href="/wiki/IGN" title="IGN">IGN</a> named <i>Scooby-Doo</i> #24 on its list of the Top 100 Best Animated TV Shows.<sup id="cite_ref-ign_101-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ign-101"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>101<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Writing in 2020, <a href="/wiki/Christopher_Orr_(film_critic)" title="Christopher Orr (film critic)">Christopher Orr</a> of <i><a href="/wiki/The_Atlantic" title="The Atlantic">The Atlantic</a></i> queried why the franchise had remained popular for several decades, concluding that it was primarily due to the many differing ways in which the relationship between the main characters could be interpreted or used as a metaphor.<sup id="cite_ref-102" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-102"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>102<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Accolades">Accolades</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=34" title="Edit section: Accolades"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>

<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Five_College_folklore">Five College folklore</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=35" title="Edit section: Five College folklore"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>A popular <a href="/wiki/Urban_legend" title="Urban legend">urban legend</a> among <a href="/wiki/Five_College_Consortium" title="Five College Consortium">Five College</a> students holds that the characters on <i>Scooby-Doo</i> represent the five colleges.<sup id="cite_ref-103" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-103"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>103<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The legend has Velma representing Smith College and Daphne as Mount Holyoke College (or vice-versa), Fred as Amherst College, Shaggy as Hampshire College, and Scooby as UMass Amherst. <a href="/wiki/Hanna-Barbera_Productions" class="mw-redirect" title="Hanna-Barbera Productions">Hanna-Barbera Productions</a>, <a href="/wiki/CBS" title="CBS">CBS</a> executive <a href="/wiki/Fred_Silverman" title="Fred Silverman">Fred Silverman</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Mark_Evanier" title="Mark Evanier">Mark Evanier</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-104" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-104"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>104<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-105" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-105"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>105<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> one of the show's writers, have stated that the legend is false.<sup id="cite_ref-106" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-106"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>106<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Moreover, <i>Scooby-Doo</i> creators <a href="/wiki/Joe_Ruby" title="Joe Ruby">Joe Ruby</a> and <a href="/wiki/Ken_Spears" title="Ken Spears">Ken Spears</a> have been explicit in the cartoon show being based on the radio program <i><a href="/wiki/I_Love_a_Mystery" title="I Love a Mystery">I Love a Mystery</a></i> and the TV sitcom <i><a href="/wiki/The_Many_Loves_of_Dobie_Gillis" title="The Many Loves of Dobie Gillis">The Many Loves of Dobie Gillis</a></i>,<sup id="cite_ref-STUEP1_6-11" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-STUEP1-6"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> with the four teenagers being based directly on characters from <i>Dobie Gillis</i>.<sup id="cite_ref-MEvanierSD_107-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-MEvanierSD-107"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>107<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In addition, <i>Scooby-Doo</i> made its television debut in 1969, one year before Hampshire College opened.<sup id="cite_ref-108" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-108"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>108<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="In_popular_culture">In popular culture</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Scooby-Doo&action=edit&section=36" title="Edit section: In popular culture"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1305433154">
<p>As with most popular franchises, <i>Scooby-Doo</i> has been parodied and has done parodies.
</p>
<ul><li>The <a href="/wiki/Cult_following" title="Cult following">cult television</a> and comic book series <i><a href="/wiki/Buffyverse" title="Buffyverse">Buffy the Vampire Slayer</a></i> features a group of characters that refer to themselves as the "Scooby Gang", who similarly battle supernatural forces and solve supernatural monster mysteries. The show contains obvious influences of <i>Scooby-Doo</i>, where "The Scoobies" use books to look up monsters. <a href="/wiki/Sarah_Michelle_Gellar" title="Sarah Michelle Gellar">Sarah Michelle Gellar</a>, the actress who plays <a href="/wiki/Buffy_Summers" title="Buffy Summers">Buffy Summers</a> on the series, later went on to appear as <a href="/wiki/Daphne_Blake" title="Daphne Blake">Daphne Blake</a> in the live-action films <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo_(film)" title="Scooby-Doo (film)">Scooby-Doo</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo_2:_Monsters_Unleashed" title="Scooby-Doo 2: Monsters Unleashed">Scooby-Doo 2: Monsters Unleashed</a></i>.<sup id="cite_ref-109" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-109"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>109<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup></li>
<li>Scooby-Doo and the Mystery Inc. gang (based on their classic 1972 incarnation as opposed to their more recent incarnations) appear in the second part of the <i><a href="/wiki/Batman:_The_Brave_and_the_Bold" title="Batman: The Brave and the Bold">Batman: The Brave and the Bold</a></i> episode "Bat-Mite Presents: Batman's Strangest Cases" in which they team up with <a href="/wiki/Batman" title="Batman">Batman</a> and <a href="/wiki/Robin_(character)" title="Robin (character)">Robin</a> to rescue <a href="/wiki/%22Weird_Al%22_Yankovic" title=""Weird Al" Yankovic">Weird Al</a> who was kidnapped by the <a href="/wiki/Joker_(character)" title="Joker (character)">Joker</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Penguin_(character)" title="Penguin (character)">Penguin</a>.</li>
<li>The song <i>Scooby-Doo and the Snowmen Mystery</i> was released in 1972 in the United Kingdom by the label <a href="/wiki/Music_for_Pleasure_(record_label)" title="Music for Pleasure (record label)">Music for Pleasure</a>.</li>
<li>The film <i><a href="/wiki/Wayne%27s_World_(film)" title="Wayne's World (film)">Wayne's World</a></i> includes an alternate ending called the "Scooby-Doo Ending" in which a character in the film is revealed to have been wearing a mask. It also includes a reference to the iconic line "Let's see who this really is" before removing the mask. When the culprit is revealed to be Old Man Withers, owner of the local haunted amusement park, Withers mutters "And I would have gotten away with it, too, if it wasn't for those meddling kids!"</li>
<li><i><a href="/wiki/Jay_and_Silent_Bob_Strike_Back" title="Jay and Silent Bob Strike Back">Jay and Silent Bob Strike Back</a></i> has a brief scene where the title characters hitch a ride in the Mystery Machine with Scooby and the gang.<sup id="cite_ref-110" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-110"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>110<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup></li>
<li>In October 1999, <a href="/wiki/Cartoon_Network" title="Cartoon Network">Cartoon Network</a> made a <i>Scooby-Doo</i> spoof of <i><a href="/wiki/The_Blair_Witch_Project" title="The Blair Witch Project">The Blair Witch Project</a></i> called <i><a href="/wiki/The_Scooby-Doo_Project" title="The Scooby-Doo Project">The Scooby-Doo Project</a></i>.<sup id="cite_ref-111" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-111"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>111<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup></li>
<li>The <i><a href="/wiki/The_Venture_Bros." title="The Venture Bros.">Venture Bros.</a></i> episode "¡Viva los Muertos!" features a thinly parodied version of the gang as aging, gone-to-seed miscreants with the characters matched to corresponding serial killers and radical figures, e.g. Fred being mixed with <a href="/wiki/Ted_Bundy" title="Ted Bundy">Ted Bundy</a> into the composite character "Ted".</li>
<li>The series is parodied in the animated music video for the song "<a href="/wiki/Ghost_(Mystery_Skulls_song)" title="Ghost (Mystery Skulls song)">Ghost</a>" by <a href="/wiki/Mystery_Skulls" class="mw-redirect" title="Mystery Skulls">Mystery Skulls</a>.</li>
<li>The <a href="/wiki/Animated_series" title="Animated series">animated series</a> <i><a href="/wiki/Arthur_(TV_series)" title="Arthur (TV series)">Arthur</a></i> has a parody of <i>Scooby-Doo</i> called "<a href="/wiki/List_of_Arthur_characters" title="List of Arthur characters">Spooky-Poo</a>".</li>
<li>In the <i><a href="/wiki/South_Park" title="South Park">South Park</a></i> episode "<a href="/wiki/Korn%27s_Groovy_Pirate_Ghost_Mystery" title="Korn's Groovy Pirate Ghost Mystery">Korn's Groovy Pirate Ghost Mystery</a>", the nu metal band <a href="/wiki/Korn" title="Korn">Korn</a>, parodying Scooby and the gang, tackle an invasion of mysterious "Pirate Ghosts". They enlist the help of <a href="/wiki/Stan_Marsh" title="Stan Marsh">Stan Marsh</a>, <a href="/wiki/Kyle_Broflovski" title="Kyle Broflovski">Kyle Broflovski</a>, <a href="/wiki/Eric_Cartman" title="Eric Cartman">Eric Cartman</a> and <a href="/wiki/Kenny_McCormick" title="Kenny McCormick">Kenny McCormick</a>, and after they solve the mystery they perform "<a href="/wiki/Falling_Away_from_Me" title="Falling Away from Me">Falling Away from Me</a>" from their album <i><a href="/wiki/Issues_(Korn_album)" title="Issues (Korn album)">Issues</a></i>.</li>
<li>In the 2003 live-action/animated film <i><a href="/wiki/Looney_Tunes:_Back_in_Action" title="Looney Tunes: Back in Action">Looney Tunes: Back in Action</a></i> an animated Scooby-Doo and Shaggy Rogers (voiced by <a href="/wiki/Frank_Welker" title="Frank Welker">Frank Welker</a> and <a href="/wiki/Casey_Kasem" title="Casey Kasem">Casey Kasem</a> respectively) argued to <a href="/wiki/Matthew_Lillard" title="Matthew Lillard">Matthew Lillard</a> over his portrayal of Shaggy in the <a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo_(film)" title="Scooby-Doo (film)">2002 live-action film</a> and threatens to "come after" him if he screws up <a href="/wiki/Scooby-Doo_2:_Monsters_Unleashed" title="Scooby-Doo 2: Monsters Unleashed">in the sequel</a>.</li>
<li>The gang was featured in <i><a href="/wiki/Harvey_Birdman,_Attorney_at_Law" title="Harvey Birdman, Attorney at Law">Harvey Birdman, Attorney at Law</a></i> where the <a href="/wiki/Harvey_Birdman" title="Harvey Birdman">title character</a> defends Shaggy and Scooby against possession charges in the 2002 episode "Shaggy Busted".</li>
<li>After defeating and capturing a pirate crew in the role playing video game <i><a href="/wiki/Golden_Sun:_The_Lost_Age" title="Golden Sun: The Lost Age">Golden Sun: The Lost Age</a></i>, one of the imprisoned pirates declares that, "Everything would have been fine if it hadn't been for you meddling kids!"</li>
<li>In the <i><a href="/wiki/Teen_Titans_Go!" title="Teen Titans Go!">Teen Titans Go!</a></i> episode "The Cruel Giggling Ghoul", each Titan assumes the role of a Scooby Gang member (with <a href="/wiki/Beast_Boy" title="Beast Boy">Beast Boy</a> as Scooby) to investigate a mystery at a spooky amusement park, with the help of <a href="/wiki/LeBron_James" title="LeBron James">LeBron James</a>. The Scooby Gang later appears in the crossover episode "Cartoon Feud", where <a href="/wiki/Control_Freak_(Teen_Titans)" class="mw-redirect" title="Control Freak (Teen Titans)">Control Freak</a> forces them to compete in <i><a href="/wiki/Family_Feud" title="Family Feud">Family Feud</a></i>. The Scooby Gang later appears in the episodes "Intro", "Warner Bros. 100th Anniversary" and "Favorite Animated Show Nominee".</li>
<li>The novel <i>Meddling Kids</i> (2017) by <a href="/wiki/Edgar_Cantero" title="Edgar Cantero">Edgar Cantero</a> parodies not only <i>Scooby-Doo</i>, but also teen-detective dramas (such as <a href="/wiki/The_Hardy_Boys" title="The Hardy Boys">the Hardy Boys</a>, <a href="/wiki/Nancy_Drew" title="Nancy Drew">Nancy Drew</a>, and <a href="/wiki/The_Famous_Five_(novel_series)" class="mw-redirect" title="The Famous Five (novel series)">the Famous Five</a>) in general.</li>
<li>The CW's television series <i><a href="/wiki/Supernatural_(American_TV_series)" title="Supernatural (American TV series)">Supernatural</a></i> crossed over with the <i>Scooby-Doo</i> franchise in the episode <i><a href="/wiki/Scoobynatural" title="Scoobynatural">Scoobynatural</a></i>, which aired March 29, 2018. The animated collaboration featured the three main characters of <i>Supernatural</i> (<a href="/wiki/Sam_Winchester" title="Sam Winchester">Sam</a>, <a href="/wiki/Dean_Winchester" title="Dean Winchester">Dean</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Castiel_(Supernatural)" title="Castiel (Supernatural)">Castiel</a>) along with Scooby and the gang as they team up to solve a supernatural mystery.<sup id="cite_ref-112" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-112"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>112<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup></li>
<li>Velma made a cameo appearance in <i><a href="/wiki/The_Lego_Movie_2:_The_Second_Part" title="The Lego Movie 2: The Second Part">The Lego Movie 2: The Second Part</a></i>, voiced by Trisha Gum.</li>
<li>The <i><a href="/wiki/Harvey_Street_Kids" class="mw-redirect" title="Harvey Street Kids">Harvey Street Kids</a></i> episode "Crush 4U, Where RU?" fully references the <i>Scooby-Doo</i> series, especially the title.</li>
<li>Scooby-Doo and the gang appear in the 2021 live-action/animated film <i><a href="/wiki/Space_Jam:_A_New_Legacy" title="Space Jam: A New Legacy">Space Jam: A New Legacy</a></i>. Their design is the same from 2020 animated film <i><a href="/wiki/Scoob!" title="Scoob!">Scoob!</a></i> They appear among the other Warner Bros. characters in the film.</li>
<li>Scooby-Doo and Shaggy both appeared in "<a href="/wiki/The_Official_BBC_Children_in_Need_Medley" title="The Official BBC Children in Need Medley">The Official BBC Children in Need Medley</a>" in 2009.</li>
<li>In the <i><a href="/wiki/Black_Mirror" title="Black Mirror">Black Mirror</a></i> episode "<a href="/wiki/Loch_Henry" title="Loch Henry">Loch Henry</a>", a character sings a line from the opening theme of <i>Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!</i> when investigating a cellar where murders had taken place.</li>
<li>The term "Don't have a Scooby" is recognised <a href="/wiki/Rhyming_slang" title="Rhyming slang">rhyming slang</a> for "clue".<sup id="cite_ref-113" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-113"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>113<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup></li>
<li>The Scooby Gang appeared in the <i><a href="/wiki/Jellystone!" title="Jellystone!">Jellystone!</a></i> third-season episode "Frankenhooky". They tie up the <a href="/wiki/Goober_and_the_Ghost_Chasers" title="Goober and the Ghost Chasers">Ghost Chasers</a> with a rope before unmasking them to reveal Sooey Pig, Orful Octopus, and Magic Rabbit of the <a href="/wiki/Really_Rottens" class="mw-redirect" title="Really Rottens">Really Rottens</a>. The Scooby Gang are revealed to actually be <a href="/wiki/Cindy_Bear" title="Cindy Bear">Cindy Bear</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ranger_Smith" title="Ranger Smith">Ranger Smith</a>, <a href="/wiki/Hardy_Har_Har" class="mw-redirect" title="Hardy Har Har">Hardy Har Har</a>, Tubb, and a cotton ball in a jar.</li>
<li>UK band, <a href="/wiki/The_Chrysanthemums_(band)" title="The Chrysanthemums (band)">The Chrysanthemums</a>, released the album <i>Decoy for a Dognapper</i> in 2022. It is a concept album, loosely based on the <a href="/wiki/Decoy_for_a_Dognapper" class="mw-redirect" title="Decoy for a Dognapper">Scooby-Doo episode</a> that it takes its title from.</li>
<li>The Scooby gang appeared in <i><a href="/wiki/Fortnite" title="Fortnite">Fortnite</a></i> during the 2025 <i>Fortnitemares</i> event from October 9–31. Each member was available as skins, and the Mystery Machine was available as a vehicle.<sup id="cite_ref-114" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-114"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>114<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup></li></ul>

# Scooby-Doo
**Scooby-Doo** (often written as **Scooby-Doo!**) is an American media franchise owned by Warner Bros. Entertainment and created in 1969 by writers Joe Ruby and Ken Spears through their animated series, Scooby-Doo, Where Are You! , for Hanna-Barbera, which was later absorbed into Warner Bros. Animation in 2001. The series features four teenagers: Fred Jones, Daphne Blake, Velma Dinkley, and Shaggy Rogers, and their talking Great Dane, Scooby-Doo, who solve mysteries involving supposedly supernatural creatures through a series of antics and missteps, while traveling in a brightly colored van called the Mystery Machine. The franchise has numerous shows, films, and specials.
Scooby-Doo was originally broadcast on CBS from 1969 to 1976, when it moved to ABC. ABC aired various versions of Scooby-Doo until canceling it in 1986, and presented a spin-off featuring the characters as children called A Pup Named Scooby-Doo from 1988 to 1991. Two Scooby-Doo reboots aired as part of Kids' WB on The WB and its successor The CW from 2002 to 2008. Further reboots aired on Cartoon Network from 2010 to 2018. Repeats of the various Scooby-Doo series are frequently broadcast on Cartoon Network's sister channel Boomerang in the United States and other countries. The most recent Scooby-Doo series, Scooby-Doo and Guess Who? , premiered on June 27, 2019, as an original series on Boomerang's streaming service and later HBO Max. 
In 2013, TV Guide ranked Scooby-Doo the fifth-greatest TV cartoon of all time.
